entry.title: Consoling Arithmetic
entry.content:
“It is consoling that the injustice of the world seems to be merely a matter of arithmetic.” —- Kafka

There is usually a common move in critical writing: it spends a long stretch analyzing a structural, political problem, lays out its historical and geographical conditions, and then in the conclusion, relocates the solution to a different level — individual cognition, say, or school curricula. This level has two features: actionable, available to be written up as concrete recommendations; does not touch the structure the analysis has just examined. I will call this move displacement, and nearly all writing of this kind ends this way.

For instances: Kimura’s gendered scientization: a political question about the distribution of power is recast as a technical one, handed to experts to adjudicate, so that the structure producing the problem is no longer held to account. The deficit model: it assumes the public fails to act because it does not know enough, so the problem becomes one of communication, make the science clear enough and action will follow; its real effect is to shift responsibility from government onto media and education, which is the same step as scientization. Decolonial scholarship: having analyzed land and sovereignty, it almost always concludes that schools should add more decolonial curriculum. The three are one move, differing only in where they land, and the decolonial case is the clearest because what gets analyzed is a historically sedimented arrangement of power, while what gets prescribed is a change in individual cognition. Curriculum becomes the default answer since it satisfies two conditions at once: it can be written as an “action recommendation,” and it will not actually alter the structure exposed.

Haraway has a line, that objects should be figured as actors and agents, not as screens, grounds, or resources. Applied to the deficit model: the way it regards “the public” is the same as the way extractive development regards land and indigenous people, both treat the other as a background or a fillable resource rather than as an agent with a standpoint of its own. So the remedy on both sides is the same: instead of speaking more loudly, we should recognize that the other was an actor all along. The difference between the Guardian and the BBC can be read against this criterion, though the conclusion is not simple. The Guardian, reporting on the environment, lets indigenous communities speak as subjects; the BBC, in the name of neutrality, piles on hedges and leaves the same communities in the background. By the actor/agent criterion the Guardian does better. But the BBC is not being lazy as well; it is just obeying a different criterion, neutrality and comprehensiveness. This shows that figuring an object as an actor is not free, as it requires choosing a standpoint, and choosing a standpoint sacrifices neutrality. The two criteria conflict here, so one cannot simply say everyone should follow the Guardian (or BBC).

Displacement and de-agentification look opposite: one assigns too much agency to the individual (you should learn more, schools should teach more), the other denies the object any agency at all. They are in fact two ends of a single problem, and what matters is not the amount of agency but where it is placed. Scientization and the deficit model place agency in the isolated individual; extractive development places it in “the one who decides.” Both assume agency is a property of discrete units that can be counted off and summed, and to sum them, one must first take the units as commensurable, as homogeneous and differing only in quantity; both therefore deny another possibility that agency is distributed across relations, and that the relation precedes each of the individuals within it. So Haraway’s line is an ontological claim, which the deficit model and coloniality both refuse.

This distinction handles two places that were otherwise stuck. First, “the land should be no one’s to decide” sounds right but turns out unusable, because whoever says it still treats the land as an object to be decided about; if the land is an actor, then “protect it or develop it” are two framings that both treat the land as a resource, and the difference lies not in which you choose but in the position of “being decided about” itself, which makes it the same kind of problem as the deficit model rather than an impasse with no way through. Second, the affective turn. Studies show that more knowledge does not produce more action, while people with a kinship or religious connection to nature are more willing to protect it; for example climate melancholia: grief over the environment drives protection. But affect does not automatically avoid displacement, if kinship means “the individual should feel a little more,” it is only the deficit model with facts swapped for feelings, agency still lodged in the isolated individual; only when kinship means “the human was always already inside a web of relations shared with non-human actors” does it land on the side of relation. The criterion throughout is where agency is placed, not how strong the feeling is.

The judgment now has to be turned on this writing itself. If I say “the problem is that agency has been put in the wrong place, and we should adopt a relational ontology,” then I am performing the very move described at the outset: a political problem about land and the distribution of power ends up relocated onto “switching to another ontology.” This landing point is even safer than curriculum, since curriculum at least has to fight for teaching hours and funding, whereas a change of ontology demands nothing and disturbs no existing arrangement. “We need a relational worldview” may be the easiest to say and the least threatening kind of displacement there is. This cannot be avoided by more careful phrasing, that critique must land somewhere, and any landing point is easier to reach than the structure it criticizes.

The Guardian’s rewriting of David Attenborough — pointing out that he is not only an environmental public figure but also an advocate of radical economic redistribution — made a flattened image complex again. That is complete in itself because it does not need “did it change anyone’s behavior” to confirm it. In Austin’s terms, this is the illocutionary effect; action belongs to the perlocutionary, a contingent aftereffect. The deficit model’s error is to fuse the two, assuming that informing necessarily yields behaviour change. That knowledge does not bring action while kinship does is the counterexample to this fusion. Separating the two lets one say both that the deficit model’s efficacy assumption is arbitrary and that the article nonetheless has value.

But this distinction also has its own politics: the media can use it to deflect that “our job is to make things clear; action is someone else’s business”, which is again a transfer of responsibility. So whoever uses it must also admit it can be used this way.

And there is a more awkward problem. Can an illocutionary effect stand on its own, apart from reception? If making an image complex is received by no one, and if most people now no longer know who Attenborough is, then was anything accomplished at all? This shows that the illocutionary too quietly assumes a condition of reception, that is, a web of relations. In other words, even this seemingly clean distinction cannot escape the relational premise set out earlier: production counts only if there is consumption.

Back to Kafka’s line. “Arithmetic” here carries two senses. The first is the consoling one: if injustice is a ledger, then position is contingent, you were not singled out by some essence or fate, you just ame up at this number; discrimination, accordingly, is not the essence of any category but a quantity assigned by position, addable and subtractable, and an account that sums this way can be re-summed that way, so no one stays on top forever. The second is the violent one: to write a person into an account is to treat them as a countable, replaceable unit, and the living dead (those who exist only as quantity and can therefore be both managed and discarded) are therefore produced.

These are two ends of one operation, joined by the commensurability of units: only once people have been reduced to homogeneous units differing solely in quantity can addition and comparison take place at all (sociology calls this process commensuration, after Espeland and Stevens). Commensurability is what the earlier methodological individualism looks like at the level of the unit, to treat value or agency as a sum of parts, one must first delete from each part whatever is non-substitutable and cannot be entered as a quantity. So the consolation of the first sense and the violence of the second buy the same thing that position can be re-summed only because the person has first been made into a re-summable unit. Consolation is capture because being consoled is itself consent to that commensuration.

The opposite logic is the line, if one being is not delivered, no being is delivered. Its point is not sameness in the sense of “equality”, that “sameness” is just commensurability, everyone the same unit. Its point is incommensurability, deliverance cannot be broken into separate deliverances summed together, and no scale lets one person’s being-delivered offset another’s not-being-delivered, so salvation is either whole or it does not hold. The equality of all beings here is not that each is an identical share but that no one is a share. This is what a relational ontology says in an older language, that a relation is not a sum of units.

Finally, back to the conflict I set aside. To write an object as an actor, one must choose a standpoint; to be comprehensive and neutral, one must suspend it. The two requirements pull against each other, with the BBC’s hedges and the Guardian’s partiality each holding one end. How many studies or reports manage both? The question should not be answered with a tidy synthesis, because it is the cost of putting a relational ontology into practice. Once you grant something a standpoint, it becomes hard to stay neutral. Thus, I will not offer a solution here, because by the logic above, any “solution” too easily becomes one more displacement.

entry.title: 夏花 | Summer Flower
entry.content:
中文版

床铺和天花板的距离太近了。陈瑞霖戴上眼镜，一层蚊帐后，白墙上斑纹点点。尖刺不足以划破喉咙，比锉平的指甲还无害。玫瑰的头开始下垂，原来它也有和瑞蓝西村的小孩一样的扁头。花瓣边缘沾上黑边，和老电影的白色噪点。花内包裹廉价酒店的大红沙发皮，陈瑞霖两指拔开，然而只是看见更嫩、更多的褶皱。他停下动作，双手握住离沙沙的叶子最远的花柄。玫瑰在胸前。

一旁的风扇灰绿地伫立。他突然想找一捆绳子，把自己拴在上面，再从床上跳下。高中时设想过类似的，如果旋转的风扇掉下，会不会正好把脑袋切掉？笔在右手里不停转动。清楚记得第一节语文课就捏过扁平的小钱包了，于是一心只想回家，走过灯红酒绿的步行街。关门，门背后总挂一块“金榜题名”的冰箱贴。”你摔门给谁看的，啊？““吃饭吧，霖子，我给你下点面条子喝吧。”“怎么了啊，霖子，怎么光吃面不吃菜啊？”“哎呀爱吃吃不吃回去。“”怎么了这是，哭了？没考好？“

老妈坐在电视机前，身体煞白。老爸的脸在灯下极为恐怖，眼下垂挂两颗漆黑的阴影，附着在眼袋上。他们都看着他。

“答应考好就给我买手机…又说话不算数。“他埋头挑起一缕面。

“你还给我提这个手机，啊？”“别、别骂霖子了。”“你知不知道现在经济不景气？！你妈不工作在家专门养你，我拼死拼活的我赚钱容易啊，还被你甩上脸色了…都是让人惯的！“

筷子飞到天上，老妈老爸开始说悄悄话。“孩子现在上学都累…““你看看那月末工资单…”

三年过去，高考刚好到黄昌大学的分数线。他离开瑞蓝。初到的烈日炎炎，在更大更空洞的黄昌上奔跑。陈瑞霖想起在议论文里经常引用的“生如夏花之绚烂”。

如果陈瑞霖知道如今境地，他绝对不会那天，开学第二周，同意加张馨云的微信。不，他连食堂都不会去。张馨云在食堂偷拍他的那张，已经被贴在记忆的耻辱柱最顶端了。

大二，家里开始给不起足够生活费，于是导员给了他一份代课的工作。当然是赚多少花多少。期末周没课可代了，好歹招生会邀请了他，给点酬劳，说是因为他德智体美劳全面发展。张馨云说：“就是你长得帅。你看你绩点才多少。”

“我还是篮球队的。”

“哎呀，我的小猫可爱吧，”张馨云转过屏幕，“它是银渐层和蓝猫杂交。”

“银渐层和蓝猫很贵的。”

“很贵吗？”

他突然不敢说话了。仓鼠的身影一闪而过，然而似乎毫无联系。

“不过是我小姨家的。”她不知想了什么。他为解读不出她的反应而更加害怕。

张馨云曾送继弟一只仓鼠。继弟并不喜欢，丢给姨妈养。猫是张馨云觉得可爱就借来的，她老说没钱，所以陈瑞霖从来不问到底买的哪种猫粮猫砂。爱一条生命，就要给它最好的，见不得它有受伤的可能，不是吗？然而他无法说出这句话。一旦说出，必然要质疑：那他没有给张馨云最好的，是不爱她吗；父母打骂他，是不爱他吗；如果爱，那为何知道疼痛还要捅破那层膜，为何没有不停工作，把钱都倾注她身上？

约会好遥远。“崔丽娥每次约会都是她对象买单，平时水果奶茶都是他花钱，他家里知道还给他恋爱补贴。然后每个月，他还寄一箱大快递，里面垫拉菲草，好多她喜欢吃的零食和衣服、盲盒。“

“哇。”他见过每次张馨云都要发过来的视频。崔丽娥像钻进稻草窝的小白狗似的。她高悬的皎洁，配上张馨云在一旁的黏腻声调，都让他不忍心地眯起眼。

“哼，我也想要，好不好嘛。人家谈女朋友都是当个宝捧在心上。我突然发现我这周给你点外卖都花了五十，难道我就很有钱吗？我给你点二十的奶茶，你连两块钱的冰淇淋都不能给我买。办法总是有的，只不过你根本没想着给我，我也明明说了自己想吃。你在你室友面前对我有哪一点能看出来我是你对象？“

“我买不起…“

“还有学习一定要我带着你学，你上一门已经考差了，这一门依然没有状态。这个游戏打完了是会有下一个游戏的，你还记得大一的时候怎么跟我说的，你说你不爱玩游戏，只偶尔跟室友打，我理解游戏是维持室友关系的一种方式，但还有不少游戏你都是自己在玩吧，之前说什么有我在时游戏都不重要，现在慢慢在我面前就是打游戏，我们一起上课是可以一句话都不说的，我们俩之间夹了一个崔丽娥你也不会想办法坐过来，如果是我的话我一定会去坐你身边。“

“崔丽娥跟我说她也想做但是她对象一直没同意，觉得太早了，我现在想来我当时才19岁，HPV也没打，你为什么就能进去？所以这些你有上网好好看过吗？我只是飞机杯吧？之前还说什么从来不看AV，完全骗人的，男人的嘴骗人的鬼我现在是发现了，刚谈上的时候甜言蜜语说的有多好，以后打脸就有多响。”

可是，可是。当时不是你追问我好几周，我才答应的吗？

“背心不用换货了，直接退掉吧，我觉得还是穿睡衣舒服。我给你买礼物很少问你要不要，因为我是听你说过什么就给你买，你给我买的礼物是我跟你强调过我想要，除了几块钱的小礼物。你在你兄弟面前有给足我安全感吗？我跟你撒娇求你你理我吗？我就不尴尬吗？在你的观念里就是有外人在的时候我就不是你女朋友而是女生朋友了。“

“我没有呀。”

“你还能找到哪个女生肯跟你吃饭平摊，还在一起半年就跟你做，主动给你买礼物点外卖，还可以跟你室友一起打球打牌。再说学习，你的诊断书有多干净你自己知道，病生听过一节课嘛？我让你上课不听的话也可以自己看网课，你说你课后再看，你有及时看吗我请问？陈瑞霖我感觉你跟我刚认识你的时候不一样了。也许所有的感情都是这样吧，故事的开头总是这样适逢其会猝不及防，故事的结尾总是这样花开两朵天各一方。“

张馨云最后引用同样在议论文里反复出现的一句，起身摔门而去。

陈瑞霖知道她下午要去讨导员要校园拍摄欠的工资。他数数钱，决定去买花。依然是玫瑰，给她一个惊喜。

他来到导员办公室门前。张馨云还在里面，竟然传来抽泣。

“对不起，我、我其实有抑郁症…我妈妈在我高一的时候就去世了…爸爸之后就一直在换女朋友谈，还给我生了一个弟弟…我真的很需要这笔钱…“

她咆哮而出，门砸到他手肘，玫瑰从脱力的手中坠落。她没有看到门后的他，反而撞上走廊另一头的崔丽娥。她白玉兰般的身姿笼罩张馨云，素净的藕臂环住她，关切地拥哭哭啼啼的她走上楼梯。张馨云无非又在对崔丽娥添油加醋。导员追上去，叹一口气黑着脸给出两百。

陈瑞霖低头，玫瑰像爆炸了似的。一滩烂肉。

回到宿舍，打开手机，沉浸在游戏中，可以让他暂时忘记这些。不知不觉和室友玩到很晚。估计第二天上课，又听不懂老师讲的啥。他想睡觉，但是张馨云一直在怪他没听课。是他不想听吗？他是听不动了。

他躺在床上，怀里是唯一存活的一支玫瑰。他侧头看向风扇。

老师，你所说的夏花究竟是什么？

English ver.

The bunk was too close to the ceiling. Chen Ruilin put on his glasses; behind a layer of mosquito net, the white wall was dappled with specks. The thorns weren’t enough to slit a throat, more harmless than filed-down fingernails. The rose’s head began to droop; so it too had a flat head, just like the children of Ruilan’s West Village. The petal edges had taken on black rims, like the white noise of old films. Inside the flower was wrapped the crimson sofa-leather of a cheap hotel; Chen Ruilin pried it apart with two fingers, but only saw more, tenderer folds. He stopped, both hands gripping the stem where it ran farthest from the rustling leaves. The rose against his chest.

Off to the side the fan stood in grayish green. He suddenly wanted to find a length of rope, tie himself to it, and jump down from the bed. In high school he’d imagined something similar — if the spinning fan came down, would it slice his head off just right? The pen kept spinning in his right hand. He remembered clearly that by the very first Chinese lesson he’d already squeezed that flat little wallet, and so wanted nothing but to go home, walking past the gaudy, neon-lit pedestrian street. Shut the door; behind the door there always hung a “May Your Name Top the Golden List” fridge magnet. “Who’re you slamming the door for, huh?” “Eat, Lin-zi, I’ll boil you some noodles to slurp.” “What’s wrong, Lin-zi, why only noodles, no vegetables?” “Aiya, eat it if you want, if not then go back.” “What’s this now, crying? Didn’t do well on the test?”

Mom sat in front of the TV, her body deathly white. Dad’s face under the light was utterly terrifying, two pitch-black shadows hanging below his eyes, clinging to the eye-bags. They were all looking at him.

“You promised if I did well you’d buy me a phone… and went back on your word again.” He bent his head and lifted a strand of noodles.

“You’re still bringing up about this, huh?” “Don’t — don’t scold Lin-zi.” “Do you not know the economy’s in a slump right now?! Your mom doesn’t work, she stays home just to raise you, I work myself to death, you think making money’s easy? — and I get attitude thrown in my face… it’s all from being spoiled!”

The chopsticks flew up into the air; Mom and Dad started whispering. “Kids these days are so worn out from school…” “Just look at that end-of-month pay slip…”

Three years passed; his gaokao score landed just on the cutoff for Huangchang University. He left Ruilan. The blazing sun of his arrival, running across a Huangchang larger and more hollow. Chen Ruilin thought of the line he’d so often quoted in his argumentative essays: “Let life be splendid like summer flowers.”

If Chen Ruilin had known the state he’d be in now, he absolutely would not have, that day, the second week of the semester, agreed to add Zhang Xinyun on WeChat. No, he wouldn’t even have gone to the canteen. The photo Zhang Xinyun secretly took of him in the canteen had already been nailed to the very top of memory’s pillory.

Sophomore year, his family began to be unable to give him enough living expenses, so the counselor got him a substitute-teaching job. Whatever he earned, of course, he spent. During finals week there were no classes left to cover, but at least the recruitment fair invited him, paid a little, said it was because he was all-round developed in morals, intellect, body, beauty, and labor. Zhang Xinyun said: “It’s just that you’re good-looking. Look how low your GPA is.”

“I’m on the basketball team too.”

“Aiya, isn’t my kitty cute,” Zhang Xinyun turned the screen around, “a cross between a silver shaded and a British Blue.”

“Silver shadeds and British Blues are expensive.”

“Are they expensive?”

He suddenly didn’t dare speak. The image of a hamster flashed past, though it seemed to have no connection.

“It’s only my aunt’s, anyway.” She was thinking who knows what. That he couldn’t decode her reaction frightened him all the more.

Zhang Xinyun had once given her stepbrother a hamster. The stepbrother didn’t like it and dumped it on their aunt to raise. The cat she’d borrowed just because she found it cute; she was always saying she had no money, so Chen Ruilin never asked what kind of cat food or litter she actually bought. To love a living thing is to give it the best, to be unable to bear the chance of its being hurt, isn’t it? But he couldn’t say this. Once said, it would inevitably raise the question: then his not giving Zhang Xinyun the best, was that not loving her; his parents beating and scolding him, was that not loving him; if it was love, then why, knowing the pain, still break through that membrane, why not work without stopping and pour all his money onto her?

Dating felt so far away. “Cui Li’e, every date, her boyfriend foots the bill; the fruit, the milk tea, day to day, he pays for all of it; his family knows and even gives him a dating allowance. And then, every month, he ships a big parcel, raffia padding inside, full of the snacks she likes and clothes, blind boxes.”

“Wow.” He’d seen the videos Zhang Xinyun forwarded him every single time. Cui Li’e was like a little white dog burrowing into a straw nest. Her luminous whiteness, suspended on high, paired with Zhang Xinyun’s clingy, cloying tone beside it, made him narrow his eyes, unable to bear it.

“Hmph, I want that too, okay? Other people, when they’ve got a girlfriend, hold her like a treasure in their heart. I suddenly realized I spent fifty just ordering you takeout this week, is it like I’m rich? I order you twenty-yuan milk tea, and you can’t even buy me a two-yuan ice cream. There’s always a way; it’s just that you never even think of me, when I clearly said I wanted some. In front of your roommates, what about you shows in any way that I’m your girlfriend?”

“I can’t afford it…”

“And studying, you always need me to carry you through it. You already did badly in the last course, and you’re still in no state for this one. When this game’s over there’ll be a next game; do you remember what you told me freshman year? You said you didn’t like games, only played with your roommates now and then. I understand games are a way to keep up with roommates, but there are plenty of games you play on your own too, right? You used to say things like, when I’m around, games don’t matter at all; now, little by little, right in front of me it’s just games. The two of us can sit through a whole class together without a single word. With a Cui Li’e wedged between the two of us, you still won’t find a way to move over and sit closer, if it were me, I’d definitely go and sit by your side.”

“Cui Li’e told me she wants to do it too, but her boyfriend never agreed, thought it was too early. Now that I think about it, I was only nineteen then, hadn’t even gotten the HPV shot, so why was it fine for you to go in? Have you actually looked any of this up online? Am I just a fleshlight? You even said you never watched porn, a complete lie. A man’s mouth, the lying devil — I’ve figured it out now: as sweet as the sweet talk was when we first got together, that’s how loud the slap to the face comes later.”

But, but. Wasn’t it you who pressed me for weeks back then, before I agreed?

“Don’t bother exchanging the tank top, just return it; I think pajamas are more comfortable anyway. When I buy you presents I rarely ask whether you want them, because I buy based on whatever you’ve mentioned; the presents you buy me are ones I’ve had to stress to you that I want, except for the few-yuan trinkets. In front of your buddies, have you ever given me enough sense of security? When I act sweet and beg you, do you even pay me any mind? Am I not embarrassed too? In your way of thinking, the moment there are outsiders around, I stop being your girlfriend and become a female friend.”

“I didn’t, though.”

“What other girl could you ever find who’d split the bill with you, who’d sleep with you after just half a year together, who’d buy you presents and order you takeout on her own, who could even play ball and cards with your roommates? And as for studying, you know yourself how clean your diagnostic report is; did you sit through even one Pathophysiology class? When I tell you not to listen in class you could at least watch the online lectures yourself; you said you’d watch them after class, and I ask you, did you watch them in time? Chen Ruilin, I feel you’re not the same as when I first met you. Maybe all relationships are like this: the beginning of the story is always like this, a chance encounter, caught off guard; the ending of the story is always like this, two flowers in bloom, each to its own far corner of the sky.”

Zhang Xinyun, in closing, quoted a line that likewise appeared again and again in argumentative essays, then stood up and slammed the door on her way out.

Chen Ruilin knew that in the afternoon she was going to the counselor to demand the wages owed her for the campus photoshoot. He counted his money and decided to go buy flowers. Roses, as ever — to give her a surprise.

He came to the door of the counselor’s office. Zhang Xinyun was still inside, and — of all things — sobbing came from within.

“I’m sorry, I — I actually have depression… my mom passed away back when I was in my first year of high school… after that my dad just kept dating one girlfriend after another, and even had a baby brother for me… I really need this money…”

She came roaring out; the door smashed into his elbow, and the rose dropped from his strengthless hand. She didn’t see him behind the door, instead she ran into Cui Li’e at the other end of the corridor. Cui Li’e’s white-magnolia figure loomed over Zhang Xinyun, her pale, lotus-root arms encircling her, and with concern she held the sniveling, weeping girl up the stairs. No doubt Zhang Xinyun was once again laying it on thick for Cui Li’e. The counselor caught up, let out a sigh, and with a darkened face handed over two hundred.

Chen Ruilin lowered his head; the rose looked as if it had exploded. A puddle of rotten flesh.

Back in the dorm, he opened his phone and sank into a game, which let him forget all this for a while. Without realizing it, he played with his roommates until late. Tomorrow in class, presumably, he’d again not understand a thing the teacher said. He wanted to sleep, but Zhang Xinyun kept blaming him for not listening in class. Was it that he didn’t want to listen? It was that he no longer had it in him to listen.

He lay on the bed, the one surviving rose in his arms. He turned his head and looked at the fan.

Teacher, what exactly is this summer flower you spoke of?

A/N

这篇和《绿》同属一个宇宙，毕竟吕缕和陈瑞霖都来自瑞蓝。并且依然是从朋友那里听来的这个故事，进行了改编。而对崔丽娥的描写的灵感来源于三岛由纪夫。顺带一提，我上个月写的《人和他的撒旦》中，付李其实毕业论文研究的就是瑞蓝，然而这是更加冗长的一个故事了。《人和他的撒旦》的篇幅过长，并且因为是第一部小说，我自觉水平不高，所以到现在都没英文翻译。

这篇我个人觉得好品的几点：

张馨云是为了博取导员的关心，才通过利用母亲的死来架起导员，让其不得不给她工资，出去和崔丽娥也是卖惨。这是真正压垮陈瑞霖的稻草，他不得不面对张馨云是一个毫无道德底线和分寸感的人，他之前一直都不愿深思张馨云对动物的不尊重、视生命如鸿毛的态度，如今他不得不面对了，她确实是连母亲的去世都要利用的人。而崔丽娥“钻进稻草窝的小白狗”和”白玉兰般的身姿……素净的藕臂”都是张瑞霖的视角，这里是说陈瑞霖和张馨云一样，都必不可免拿自己感情和其他人的比较；把丽娥看作“小白狗”，说明他在觉得她可爱的同时是在把她当作更低位的东西观赏的，“白玉兰”“藕臂”则就是单纯凝视她的外貌。就是说，他也并非全心全意喜欢张馨云，也并非只是“精神上的巨人”。

陈瑞霖永远无法达到“生如夏花”的那种高度，他永远不知道那是什么，因为他被生活的这些琐事麻痹了，如同温水煮青蛙。就像他不愿意承认张馨云是毫无底线的人，他也无法承认自己也是一个麻痹自我的人，他将永远看着风扇幻想死亡，然而第二天继续起床，听不懂课，被女朋友骂，如此捆绑、没有勇气地走过自己一生。

然而我欢迎各种其他解读，毕竟我不应给予情感。

This piece belongs to the same universe as Green, since both Lü Lü and Chen Ruilin come from Ruilan. And, as before, this is a story I heard from a friend and then adapted. The inspiration for the depiction of Cui Li’e comes from Yukio Mishima. Incidentally, in People and Their Satan, which I wrote last month, Fu Li’s thesis actually researches Ruilan, but that’s a far longer story. People and Their Satan runs too long, and since it’s my first novel I don’t think much of my own level, so to this day there’s no English translation of it.

A few things I personally find worth savoring in this piece:

Zhang Xinyun, in order to win the counselor’s sympathy, exploits her mother’s death to corner the counselor, leaving him no choice but to hand over her wages; going off with Cui Li’e is likewise a play for pity. This is the true last straw that breaks Chen Ruilin, he is forced to face that Zhang Xinyun is a person without any moral bottom line or sense of proportion. He had always been unwilling to think hard about Zhang Xinyun’s disrespect for animals, her treatment of life as light as a feather; now he has no choice but to face it, that she really is someone who would exploit even her own mother’s death. And Cui Li’e as “a little white dog burrowing into a straw nest” and as the “white-magnolia figure… pale, lotus-root arms” are both Chen Ruilin’s point of view; the point here is that Chen Ruilin, just like Zhang Xinyun, inevitably compares his own relationship against other people’s. Seeing Li’e as a “little white dog” shows that even as he finds her cute he is appraising her as something lower in position; “white magnolia” and “lotus-root arms” are simply a gaze fixed on her looks. That is to say, he does not wholeheartedly love Zhang Xinyun either, nor is he merely a “giant of the spirit.”

Chen Ruilin can never reach the height of “life splendid like summer flowers”; he will never know what it is, because he has been numbed by these trivialities of living, like a frog in slowly warming water. Just as he is unwilling to admit that Zhang Xinyun is a person without any bottom line, he is also unable to admit that he himself is a person who numbs himself; he will forever stare at the fan and fantasize about death, yet get up again the next day, fail to understand his classes, get scolded by his girlfriend, and walk through his entire life bound up like this, without courage.

That said, I welcome all manner of other readings, after all, I shouldn’t be supplying emotions.

entry.title: On Turning 20
entry.content:
Already 20. Because I had an exam on June 1st, I kept putting it off, and only today am I writing the blog post.

Come to think of it, I’d always assumed the June 1st exam would end at 16:30, but it turned out to run three hours; when I walked out of the exam hall at 17:30, although by rights the sky should still have been bright, I felt the way I did getting out of school as a child, the sky dimming down. I pulled out my nearly dead phone, ran back over the exam’s contents in my mind, had no appetite at all, and bought only a bunch of Sweet Williams.

Sweet Williams symbolize courage or manliness, and were traditionally used to describe a knight in the garden. This happens to echo the birthday illustration I received this year: a dandelion knight’s Chariot card. Dandelions are often regarded as weeds, yet they live on, inexhaustibly; the Chariot card gives me an Apollo impression: driving the brightest chariot in the vast cosmos, bursting forth toward a brighter distance. The flowers were simply the new variety the shop happened to stock that day; the illustration was the commissioned artist‘s own idea, so none of these images came from my own intent. I like this bit of coincidence, as if, on the day I turned 20, the heavens had finally answered me. Omen or dissection, whichever, these images all, inexplicably, granted me a kind of empathetic strength.

On May 17th, I finished my first novel, People and Their Satan. This is the thing I’m proudest of, because it made it in before I turned 20. I only even began conceiving it in May, though I’d had plenty of stories to tell from earlier than high school. Beyond this, there’s nothing worth mentioning.

I cannot appraise the past 20 years. Appraisal requires comparison, and I don’t know what I should compare them against.

This post is rather personal so I’ll keep it short.

entry.title: On Prefigurative Writing
entry.content:
I recently came across an introductory piece on prefigurative politics that moves between the Zapatistas, Rojava, and the MST, allotting each case under a hundred words, closing each section with a quotation from Subcomandante Marcos or bell hooks or Buckminster Fuller. It claims to introduce a politics of “means are ends.” Halfway through I realised the piece was arriving at prefigurative ends through anti-prefigurative means, and was wholly unaware of the contradiction.

If means are ends, then writing about prefiguration must itself be prefigurative. Otherwise you are using a form that betrays your politics to advertise your politics. The problem is epistemological, and it has several identifiable modes of failure.

The first: quotations carrying emotional weight rather than argumentative weight. Bell hooks wrote “what we cannot imagine cannot come into being” inside a specific lineage of Black feminist reclamation of imagination as political resource. Its function is to make the paragraph feel heavier than it actually is. Prefiguration demands that form carry its own political work; outsourcing the liberation of imagination to hooks’s name severs means from ends. Borneman’s claim that care is the source and result of human creativity holds because he spent an entire essay on the relation between Dieter and Harald, a bond unaccommodated by any kinship category, doing the work of holding it up (1997, p. 583). A quotation that does not carry its original argumentative weight is only ornament.

The second and more concealed failure: flattening different situated knowledges into homogenous inspiration. The Zapatistas’ political architecture grew from a specific suturing of Mayan cosmology and Marxist tradition; Rojava’s democratic confederalism arrived through Bookchin via Öcalan’s particular reading; the MST is embedded in the legal history of Brazilian land reform and the soil of liberation theology. Real tensions exist between the three on questions of sovereignty, scale, and relation to the state. Lining them up as “sources of inspiration,” each allotted equal word count and equal rhetorical weight, is itself an epistemic flattening. The whole stake of Haraway’s situated knowledge is that objectivity is the honest marking of a position; flattening into interchangeable case studies performs its inverse. Munhazim and Zondon, writing on queer Muslim death, insist that “living deaths” and “unlived desires” cannot be absorbed into a universal rhetoric of surviving (2021), because absorption converts structurally silenced dying into consumable “inspiration.” Yet movement-tourism writing does exactly this.

The third and most awkward failure: writing in the future tense about building that is happening now. Such pieces keep saying “we must imagine,” “we should construct”, while actual prefigurative practice has already been building. Dakar’s waste pickers are already running an alternative economy and Mbeubeuss has its own territorial divisions and governance structures. Palestinian families in Sheikh Jarrah stay daily through legal struggle and bodily presence. Packaging this ongoing building as “a future we can dream of” is a violence of tense, it demotes present-tense political work into future-tense inspirational narrative and sells the demotion as hope. Means are ends means the future is here and rewriting building as imagining pushes it back into the future.

What does prefigurative writing look like, then? Allen’s There’s a Disco Ball Between Us is a clear example. Allen writes Black gay time space by moving between the moment Kevin Aviance saw his dead girlfriends in the Palladium and the metaphor of the Atlantic as a collection of mirrors, placing the reader inside the fragmented light the disco ball throws off. The form does the political work the book claims, anti-linear ends cannot be reached by linear means, so Allen did not write linearly. The Munhazim and Zondon collaborative autoethnography works the same way: it refuses to draw a clean line between the analyst’s position and the lives being analysed, because that line is itself the epistemological violence they are protesting.

To clarify, an analytical piece, comparing how Zapatistas and Rojava conceptualise sovereignty, can perfectly well take a conventional academic form, because its ends are analytical understanding instead of prefiguration. The problem only arises when writing claims to do prefigurative political work, when the ends are sparking prefigurative practice while the means are compressing radical politics into broth, flattening situated struggle into homogenous inspiration, rewriting present-tense building as future-tense dreaming. It is in those moments, the failure of form is the failure of politics.

The argument is also a constraint on my own writing. I keep returning, in the “slopes of care” series, because if I do not let their specificity resist my generalisation, for example if I let Rukban become a case study about dereferencing rather than Rukban itself, I am performing the violence I have just described. The minimum requirement of means are ends, applied to writing, is that: do not use a form that renders its object consumable to write about conditions that are not consumable.

entry.title: 桃花源后记｜Postscript to the Peach Blossom Spring
entry.content:
A/N (Foreword)

I wrote this short play in May 2020, for a school stage performance on World Environment Day.

Re-reading it now, six years later and halfway through a degree that has taught me to be suspicious of exactly the kind of redemption arc this play stages… the structure surprised me. I have left the original text untouched, added an English translation alongside it, and written a longer afterword at the end that tries to think about what the play does and does not see, and what it might look like if I wrote it now.

The play is in classical Chinese pastiche for the fisherman and modern Mandarin for the two children, a register split that I have tried to preserve in translation by giving the fisherman an early-modern English voice (thee, thou, hath) and the children contemporary speech.

For readers unfamiliar with the source: Tao Yuanming’s Peach Blossom Spring (《桃花源记》, c. 421 CE) is one of the most canonical short pieces in Chinese literary history. A fisherman from Wuling follows a stream lined with peach blossoms and stumbles into a hidden valley whose inhabitants, refugees from the Qin dynasty wars, have lived in isolated peace for six hundred years. He can never find the way back and the valley becomes a byword for unreachable utopia.

This play is what happens after.

出场人物 / Cast

  • 武陵渔人 The Fisherman of Wuling
  • 少年甲 First Boy
  • 少年乙 Second Boy
  • 旁白 Narrator

脚本、导演、剧务 / Script, Director, Stage Management
郑旗 Zheng Qi

剧本 / Script

（旁白：） 武陵渔人自从桃花源一别，对当初在桃花源中度过的日子念念不忘。奈何遍寻不着归路，只得重操旧业，以捕鱼为生。

(NARRATOR.) Ever since his parting from the Peach Blossom Spring, the fisherman of Wuling has been unable to put those days from his mind. Yet though he has searched far and wide, no path will lead him back. He has returned to his old trade and lives by fishing.

年复一年，每逢春至，村中桃李盛开，渔人不免睹物思旧。这一日他乘着小舟，顺流而往，不料远远瞧见溪水尽头有一处山隘，桃花盛开，灿若云霞。

Year after year, each time spring comes and the peach and plum trees in his village burst into bloom, the sight stirs the old longing in him. On this particular day, drifting downstream in his small boat, he glimpses, far ahead at the end of the water, a narrow gorge between hills — and peach blossoms in full flower, glowing like sunset cloud.

（渔人讶道） “这！莫不正是那桃花源的入口？”（低头沉吟，又抬首四顾）”不，这似乎并不是上回去往桃花源的路径，罢了，还是去看看吧。”（说罢摇橹前行）

(FISHERMAN, astonished.) “Lo! Could this be none other than the gateway to the Peach Blossom Spring?” (He bows his head in thought, then looks about him.) “Nay — methinks ‘tis not the path I trod before. No matter; I shall go and see.” (So saying, he plies his oar onward.)

（旁白） 渔人一路只见落英缤纷。走近后，却见自那山隘中透出昏黄的光来。渔人系舟登岸，走近山隘向里张望。但见深处别有洞天。苍穹之下，有银色巨鸟呼啸而过。远处高楼鳞次栉比，密密匝匝仿佛要接到天边去。

(NARRATOR.) All along the way, the fisherman sees fallen petals drifting on the water. But as he draws nearer, a dim yellow light spills out from the gorge. He moors his boat, steps ashore, and approaches the opening to peer within. Within, another world entirely lies. Beneath the vault of heaven, silver birds of monstrous size go shrieking past. Far off, towers stand rank upon rank, packed close as if they would press their tops against the very edge of the sky.

渔人走入山隘，见近旁有两位奇装异服的少年，正蹲在溪水边用奇怪的透明容器取水。

The fisherman steps into the gorge, and there beside him crouch two strangely dressed youths at the stream’s edge, drawing water into queer transparent vessels.

（渔人上前）： “两位小兄弟，敢问此乃何处？尔等缘何作此装扮？”

(FISHERMAN, approaching.) “Good young sirs, pray tell me — what manner of place is this? And wherefore art thou clad in such strange attire?”

少年乙： “咦，你谁呀？你的装扮怎么这个样子？拍戏吗？”

SECOND BOY. “Huh? Who are you? Why are you dressed like that — are you filming something?”

“在下武陵人氏，为寻桃花源而来，未料误入宝地，却不知此为何处仙乡？竟如此光怪陆离？”

“Thy servant is a man of Wuling, come hither in search of the Peach Blossom Spring. By chance I have stumbled upon thy precious land, yet I know not what blessed realm this be — for ‘tis passing strange and wondrous beyond all telling.”

少年乙： “哇！武陵渔人长得就是这个样子啊？我们刚学过讲桃花源的课文！你没在骗我吧？”

SECOND BOY. “Whoa! So this is what the Wuling fisherman actually looks like? We literally just studied that text in class! You’re not pulling my leg, are you?”

少年甲推推眼镜： “如果你没有扯谎，那么这里对于你的时代来说，是一千多年后的未来。”

FIRST BOY (pushing up his glasses). “If you aren’t lying, then for your era, this place is more than a thousand years in the future.”

渔人大惊，惶然四顾：”啊！一千多年！小兄弟莫……莫要诓我！”

The fisherman is struck with dismay and looks wildly about him. “Alas! A thousand years! Young sir, do not — do not deceive me!”

少年乙掐指： “等等等等，让我来算算。”

SECOND BOY (counting on his fingers). “Hold on, hold on, let me work it out.”

少年乙背诵《朝代歌》（一边狐疑地围绕着渔人转悠，一边摇头晃脑有节奏地背诵）

(Second Boy recites the Dynasty Song, circling the fisherman with a sceptical air, head bobbing in rhythm.)

夏商周，春秋战。
秦朝以后是两汉，
三国两晋南北朝。
隋唐五代宋辽夏，
金元明清二十朝。

“Xia, Shang, Zhou — Spring and Autumn, Warring States.
After the Qin came the two Han.
Three Kingdoms, two Jins, Northern and Southern Courts.
Sui, Tang, Five Dynasties, Song, Liao, Xia,
Jin, Yuan, Ming, Qing — twenty dynasties in all.”

少年乙一拍大腿：”哎哟！算算从东晋到现在，您可是一千六百多年前的古人了。”（好奇地上下打量渔人）”这么说来，您本人可不就是个活的老古董了么？”（两眼闪闪发光）

Second Boy slaps his thigh. “Aiyo! Counting from the Eastern Jin to now, you’d be a man from over sixteen hundred years ago.” (He looks the fisherman up and down with frank curiosity.) “Which means, you’re basically a living antique!” (His eyes glitter.)

少年甲轻推少年乙，提醒他注意礼貌： “什么老古董，得尊称一声’人瑞爷爷’。”

FIRST BOY (nudging Second Boy and reminding him of his manners). “Don’t say ‘antique.’ Show some respect, call him ‘Venerable Grandfather.’”

渔人心神大震，张望四周，对两人颔首道：”二位所言不虚。若非未来，何来此等闻所未闻之景！只是，我原本自碧水青天之处而来，为何此地……”（手指颤抖着指向远处，面露惊讶）”却昏暗晦暝，竟似有雾霭遮天蔽日？就这？”

The fisherman, deeply shaken, casts his gaze about and bows his head to them. “What ye twain say must be true. Were it not the future, whence such sights as I have never beheld nor heard of? Yet — I came hither from a land of clear waters and azure skies. Why is it that here…” (With trembling finger he points into the distance, his face full of wonder.) “…all is dim and obscure, as though a fog hath veiled the very sun? Is this all there is?”

少年甲叹息： “唉，说起来，这还是人类的过错。百年来，人类社会科技和文明高速发展，人们不断地向大自然索取资源、大量使用无法降解的塑料制品、过量排放污水和热能，导致海平面上升、极地冰川融化、天空上方的臭氧层也受到波及，空气质量混浊，自然也就看不到碧水青天的景色了。”

FIRST BOY (sighing). “Ah, to tell the truth, this is humankind’s own doing. Over the past hundred years, our science and civilisation have advanced at breakneck speed. People have taken endlessly from nature, used vast quantities of plastics that will not decompose, discharged sewage and waste heat without restraint. The seas have risen; the polar ice melts; even the ozone layer overhead is wounded. The air has grown thick and foul. Of course one can no longer see clear waters and azure skies.”

渔人问： “敢问二位在此所为何事？”

FISHERMAN. “And what, pray, art thou twain doing in this place?”

少年乙举起手中的采集瓶： “我们正在采集实验数据，从自然水域中取得天然水样本，由我们班的博士级科学怪人进行分析。”（指向少年甲）

SECOND BOY (holding up his collection bottle). “We’re gathering experimental data — taking samples from natural waterways for analysis. Our class’s resident mad scientist here does the actual lab work.” (He points at First Boy.)

少年甲： “低调、低调！”（风采的动作）”从我们对这条小溪的观测结果来看，污染情况很严重。工业排放的气体和废水蒸发形成酸雨，落在附近的山坡上。”（指着附近）”你看，酸雨所经之处，植被凋零，而以草木为生的虫蚁与动物，数目也大为减少。这些酸雨和工业废水汇集到小溪中，破坏了自然水域中的生态平衡，致使水体混沌，鱼虾、微生物和藻类无法生存。”

FIRST BOY. “Modest, modest!” (Strikes a poised attitude.) “From our observations of this stream, the pollution is severe. Industrial emissions and evaporated wastewater form acid rain, which falls on the surrounding hillsides.” (He points around them.) “Look — wherever the acid rain has fallen, the vegetation withers, and the insects and animals that depend on plants have dwindled in number. This acid rain and industrial effluent drain into the stream, breaking the ecological balance of the natural water. The water grows turbid, and fish, shrimp, microorganisms, and algae can no longer survive.”

渔人： “却不知这虫蚁与动物数目、又或鱼虾，竟与环境有关？”

FISHERMAN. “I knew not that the numbers of insects and beasts, of fish and shrimp, were thus bound up with the state of their dwelling-place.”

少年乙： “当然有关啦。那些看似不起眼的小草和小昆虫，它们正是生物多样性的基础。由于人类生活领地的的扩大，许多物种绝迹。相比起您所生活的晋代，我们这个时代的生物种类已是相当贫乏。生物种类的缺失，进一步影响到生态、气候、地质结构，如果继续恶性循环下去，怕是这个世界再不能见到朗朗乾坤，碧水青天了。”（叹息）

SECOND BOY. “Of course they are! Those little plants and tiny insects that look so ordinary — they are the foundation of biodiversity. As humans have spread further and further into the wild, many species have gone extinct. Compared to your Jin dynasty, the variety of life in our time is already deeply impoverished. And the loss of species feeds back into climate, ecosystems, geological structures. If this vicious cycle continues, this world may never see bright heavens and clear waters again.” (He sighs.)

渔人： “二位可有解决之道？”

FISHERMAN. “Have ye twain any remedy?”

少年乙： “办法倒是有，但……此事并非一人能为啊。”

SECOND BOY. “There is, but… this isn’t something one person can do alone.”

渔人： “此话怎讲？”

FISHERMAN. “How meanest thou?”

少年甲（双手背后，踱步上前，面向观众）： “环境保护之道，在于众志成城。唯有每一位地球居民都身体力行地爱护环境、心存拯救地球的善念、不滥用自然资源、爱护野生动物、使用可降解材料，世界才会越来越好。”

FIRST BOY (hands clasped behind his back, pacing forward to face the audience). “The way of environmental protection lies in the union of all wills. Only when every inhabitant of this Earth, in their own person, cherishes the environment, holds in their heart the wish to save the planet, refuses to squander natural resources, protects wild creatures, and uses biodegradable materials, only then will the world grow better.”

少年乙问渔人： “嘿！对了，这位老祖宗……不不，这位人瑞爷爷，您还要回到晋代吗？”

SECOND BOY (turning to the fisherman). “Hey — by the way, ancient ancestor — I mean, Venerable Grandfather — do you still want to go back to the Jin dynasty?”

渔人回首张望来处，竟瞧不见来时路：”啊！我来时的那个山隘呢！”（着急地四处张望寻找）

The fisherman turns to look back the way he came but the path is gone. “Lo! The gorge whence I came, where is it?” (He casts about anxiously, searching.)

少年甲边思索边说： “如果您果真是来自晋代。那么您出现在这里的唯一通道就只有’时空虫洞’。根据全息原理，所有在第五维的事件可以变换为在其它四维的事件，引力与它弯曲时空的能力来自于量子纠缠。在纠缠粒子被生成的同时，时空虫洞也被生成……”（这一段语速稍快，念念有词）

FIRST BOY (speaking thoughtfully). “If you truly come from the Jin, then the only possible passage by which you arrived here is a ‘spacetime wormhole.’ According to the holographic principle, all events in the fifth dimension can be transformed into events in the other four dimensions, and gravity together with its capacity to curve spacetime arises from quantum entanglement. At the moment entangled particles are produced, a spacetime wormhole is also produced…” (He delivers this rapidly, half to himself.)

渔人摇头： “小兄弟所言，在下完全听不懂。”

FISHERMAN (shaking his head). “Of what the young sir speaks, thy servant comprehendeth not a word.”

少年乙： “他的意思是啊，量子纠缠是瞬间并且偶然发生的，时空虫洞不会随时存在。很遗憾您可能回不去了，得留在这儿。”

SECOND BOY. “What he means is, quantum entanglement happens in an instant, and by chance. The wormhole isn’t always there. Unfortunately, you probably can’t go back. You’ll have to stay here.”

渔人如释重负： “哦，那不打紧。自上回离开桃花源，在下悔不当初，错失仙缘。如今机缘巧合来到此地，不如在此好好过活。只是尚有一事未明，需向二位请教。”（抬手作揖）

FISHERMAN (with an air of relief). “Oh, that mattereth not. Since I last departed the Peach Blossom Spring, I have rued the day, having lost a divine fortune through mine own folly. Now, by some happy chance, I have come hither — better, then, that I make my dwelling here. Yet there is one thing still that puzzles me, and I would beg of ye an answer.” (He raises his hands and bows.)

少年甲少年乙回礼同答： “请说。”

FIRST BOY and SECOND BOY (returning the bow together). “Please ask.”

渔人： “在下前回误入之境被称为’桃花源’。那么，现下你我所在之境，当如何称呼？”（略思索）”莫非是……莫非是……’污染源’？”

FISHERMAN. “The realm into which I once strayed was called the Peach Blossom Spring — Tao Hua Yuan. What then, pray, is the name of this realm wherein we three now stand?” (He pauses in thought.) “Could it be… could it be… the Pollution Spring — the Wu Ran Yuan?”

少年甲少年乙相视大笑： “不。我们有信心，将我们这个世界修复成’桃花源’！”

FIRST BOY and SECOND BOY (exchanging a look and bursting into laughter). “No! We have faith, that we shall mend this world of ours back into a Peach Blossom Spring!”

三人至台前：”关爱自然，刻不容缓！”

(All three step forward to the front of the stage.) “To cherish nature, there is not a moment to lose!”

【剧终】全体演职员鞠躬道谢，退场。

[END.] The full company bows in thanks and exits.

A/N (Afterword): Reading This Six Years On

The structural choice is the strongest thing in it. The original Peach Blossom Spring is built around a movement from a debased present (the wars of the late Eastern Jin) into a recovered ideal past (a community of Qin refugees still living the agrarian peace of six centuries earlier). The fisherman crosses from the corrupted now into the preserved then. Postscript inverts this: the fisherman, already inhabiting what Tao’s text codes as the lost ideal, crosses into the corrupted future. The pastoral past now looks back at industrial modernity and finds it sick. This is an ironic, almost elegiac structural move, and it does real work, it stages climate degradation as something a pre-modern observer would find legible as harm, which is itself a quiet rebuke to the modernist story that progress has been a uniform improvement.

The register split between classical Chinese pastiche and modern Mandarin is the play’s other genuine craft achievement. The fisherman’s speech indexes a knowledge-world: bi shui qing tian (clear water and azure skies) is a literary topos, freighted with poetic use. When he asks why the sky is dim, he is registering a loss of a cosmological category. The boys’ speech, by contrast, is the diction of the school environmental curriculum: biodiversity, ecological balance, acid rain. The two characters speak from inside two different epistemic communities.

Here is where six years of reading STS and decolonial environmental thought changes what I notice.

The framing is unreflectively diffusionist. The two children are positioned as scientific knowledge-bearers and the fisherman as a recipient of explanation. He asks; they explain. This reproduces what Jasanoff would call a deficit model of public understanding: the layperson (here, the historical person) is empty, and the scientifically literate filler-in-the-blank is the source of true knowing. But the fisherman of Wuling is not epistemically empty. He is a person whose livelihood depends on detailed observational knowledge of a watershed, fish behaviour, seasonal cycles, water clarity, vegetation along banks. He would, in fact, be among the first to register an ecological wrongness in the boys’ polluted stream, and probably to do so more acutely and more quickly than they can with their sample bottles.

The pastoral ideal is left unproblematised. Postscript mobilises the Peach Blossom Spring as a pre-political baseline of ecological health that modernity has fallen away from, and that we should “repair the world back into.” But the Tao Hua Yuan is not actually an ecological vision; it is a refugee fantasy of a community that has withdrawn from history. Its “harmony with nature” is a side-effect of low population density and pre-industrial productive technology, not an intentional environmental ethic. To read it as a sustainability template is to perform what Hulme has called the moralisation of climate, the conversion of a complex socio-technical situation into a fall-and-redemption narrative.

Co-production is missing. Following Jasanoff, the production of scientific knowledge and the production of social order are mutually constitutive: who counts as a knower, what counts as an observation, which forms of evidence are legible, and they are made together with the political and institutional arrangements that authorise them. The boys’ sample bottle is an artefact of a specific epistemic regime (laboratory analysis, instrumented quantification, the school science curriculum). The fisherman’s idiom of bi shui qing tian is an artefact of another (literary memory, observation embedded in classical poetics). The play has both regimes on stage and could have staged the encounter between them as the actual drama. Instead it lets the modern regime narrate the encounter and reduces the older one to a figure of innocence.

The fisherman’s affect is wrong. He arrives in a polluted future and accepts staying with relief. This makes no sense for the character the original text gives us, a man defined by not being able to find his way back to a beloved place.

entry.title: 好 | Granted
entry.content:
中文版

曾经他们胡须攒动，交错间一根指向月，一根指向日。其间天地都是他们的。

“我我我…我把女儿嫁给你！最漂亮的那个！求求你，放我一条生路…”

那样宽敞的天地，怎么会如今都没有生路。

猫咧出一条细长的嘴型，说一声”好”，终于走了。

猫说：”结婚算不算大喜事，要分情况看。比如我们。

“天宫十二生肖选举那天我等你爸等得好苦，你爸却抛下我一人，偷偷跑了，又偷偷藏进牛角里。你爸在那遥远的天宫得了第一，而我还守在人间的树洞里等着他，等着他，等着他出现，直到那比赛结果都出来，我都不敢相信选举已经结束了。蛇说你爸这是聪明，牛好脾气解释这是任何动物都有闪光点；可我要证明他们都错了。恶就应该有恶报。我说’我们明明答应一起去，你却言而无信，害我本有比赛资格却失去机会，你就这样想赢，想要名垂千古？你该如何偿还这回不来的光阴和信任？’你爸说’我把最漂亮的女儿嫁给你。’

“首先，这不足以偿还任何东西。不是说你没有价值，恰恰是因为你，你是无法衡量的，不应该被用来交换的，你也不是他的所有物。其次，你的外貌、种族、性别都和我毫无关系，你和我结婚在我看来对我没有好处，对你没有好处。你爸偏偏选了最荒谬的偿还方式。当然，他选其他的也是偿还不够的。我如何复仇也是不够的。因为我失去的也无法衡量和回来。”

“猫，可是我的鼠生还要继续。”

猫看向妻子：”哦，可是你的鼠生已经既定了，不是吗。想象一下，我在能同时杀了你、你的兄弟姐妹、你妈和你爸的情况下，你爸选择了推出谁去牺牲？接下来我要是吃了你，他要继续推谁去给他挡灾？最后棋盘上只会有我和你爸。在那之前你们就是你爸的棋子。好孩子，不要哭，我想为你解释清楚，你是不可避免的一环。而且，我饿了。比赛过后我一无所有。绝望是空洞的，占满了整个大脑，我停不下来，反复想这一切怎么发生，怎么收场。只有与食物的接触是我与世界最直接无害的联系了。”

猫残忍杀害了眼前的老鼠。他砍下她的头，嗦出脖颈的血汁，接着是手臂，一口口吞下肚腩里的器官花园，最后一饮而尽头颅里剩下的所有液体。

剪下她的胡须，撒在鼠的门前。

这是我们的天地，一根指向过去，一根指向未来。

鼠在门后隐隐听见风声。冬日的风有着刮骨寒凉的气息，递来猫的呓语——我答应过你，满足你所有愿望，你既说要生，我便让你生。

从此你将只剩下生。

English Ver.

Their whiskers once bristled in tandem, crossing in the space between, one pointing toward the moon, one toward the sun. All the world between was theirs.

“I – I – I’ll marry my daughter to you! The most beautiful one! Please, I’m begging you, spare me, let me live – “

So vast, that world had been. How is it that now there is no way out alive.

Cat stretched his mouth into a long, thin shape, said “deal,” and finally left.

Cat said: “Whether a wedding counts as a joyous occasion, that depends. Take ours.

“The day of the Heavenly Court’s great zodiac race, I waited for your father until it ached. Your father abandoned me, slipped away in secret, and hid himself inside Ox’s horn. Your father stood in that faraway celestial palace and took first place, while I was still in my hollow in the earth, waiting for him, waiting for him, waiting for him to appear, until the results were announced and I still could not believe the race was already over. Snake called your father clever; Ox, good-tempered, explained that every animal has a redeeming quality; but I would prove them all wrong. Evil should be repaid in kind. I said: we agreed to go together, and you broke your word, you robbed me of my rightful place; you wanted to win that badly, to have your name last through the ages? How will you repay the time and the trust that will never return? Your father said: I will marry my most beautiful daughter to you.

“First, this is not enough to repay anything. Not because you have no worth, but precisely because you do; you are immeasurable, you should never be exchanged, and you are not his to give. Second, your appearance, your species, your sex, none of it concerns me; this marriage does me no good and does you no good. Your father chose the most absurd form of repayment, though of course any other form would also have fallen short, and any revenge of mine would also fall short, because what I lost is equally immeasurable and equally irrecoverable.”

“Cat, but my life still has to go on.”

Cat turned to his wife: “Oh, but your life has already been decided, hasn’t it. Consider: when I could have killed you, your siblings, your mother, and your father all at once, who did your father choose to push forward? And once I have eaten you, who will he push out next to take the blow? In the end the board holds only me and your father; until then, you are all his pieces. Good child, don’t cry, I want to make this clear to you, you are an inevitable step. Also, I’m hungry. After the race I had nothing; the despair was hollow, it filled my entire skull, and I could not stop turning it over, how it all happened, how it all ends. The only contact with the world that still felt direct and harmless was the contact with food.”

Cat killed the mouse before him with savage precision. He severed her head, drew the blood from the neck in one long pull, then the arms, swallowed mouthful by mouthful the organ garden inside the belly, and drank to the last drop every liquid left in the skull.

He cut off her whiskers and scattered them at Rat’s door.

This is our world, one pointing toward the past, one toward the future.

Behind the door, Rat heard the wind faintly. The winter wind carried a bone-scraping cold, delivering Cat’s murmur – I promised to grant your every wish; you asked to live, so I let you live.

From now on, living is all you will have left.

A/N: Happy April Fools’. In the Chinese zodiac origin myth, Rat and Cat agreed to travel together to the Jade Emperor’s great race which would decide the twelve zodiac animals. Rat broke that promise and he slipped away in the night, hid inside Ox’s horn, and leapt ahead to claim first place. Cat never arrived because he was waiting for the Rat. That is why, the story goes, cats hunt rats to this day.

In the fuller version of the story, Cat later comes to collect, and Rat, desperate, offers his most beautiful daughter in marriage, and Cat eventually devours her. Here I change only the consciousness inside it. I wanted the most lucid analysis in the story to belong to the one who devours, therefore showing that seeing clearly and doing right are not the same thing.

Rat begged for a way to live and Cat said yes. The April Fools’ trick for this one is that there was no trick! Every word was true and every deal was honoured.

entry.title: Boundary Work and the Dialectics of Platform Identity
entry.content:
A Reflection on Cammaerts’ Dichotomies in Media and Communication Theory

At the launch of his new textbook on 31 March 2026, Bart Cammaerts opened with a scene from this same LSE theatre. Keynes and Hayek in 1931, locked in a debate whose very structure, binary, adversarial, performed as intellectual duel, became his object of inquiry. The book maps eight dichotomies that organise media and communication studies, and Cammaerts’ central provocation is methodological. He refuses to resolve these tensions, arguing instead for inhabiting “the lure of the middle,” a position he describes as dialectical rather than conciliatory. Two contradictory things, he insists, can be true at the same time.

This claim has a longer genealogy than Cammaerts’ own framing through Gramsci, Mouffe, and Foucault might suggest. The symmetry principle in Bloor’s strong programme makes a structurally analogous move, demanding that we explain “true” and “false” knowledge claims using the same causal apparatus, suspending the epistemological privilege that would let us dismiss one side of a dichotomy in advance. Where Cammaerts applies this logic to political economy versus cultural studies, or Habermasian rationalism versus agonistic democracy, GY220 applies it to technological determinism versus social constructivism.

The terrain matters, because Cammaerts’ most compelling empirical material turns out to be legible in STS terms in ways that exceed his own theoretical vocabulary. Platforms, he argues, are simultaneously media and communication infrastructure. They make editorial decisions through algorithmic curation while claiming the legal status of neutral conduits modelled on the telephone network. This double identity allows them to evade the regulatory obligations imposed on legacy media. Cammaerts reads this as ideological manoeuvre. Read through Gieryn’s concept of boundary work, the analysis sharpens. Platform companies are drawing and redrawing the boundary between “media” and “communication tool” depending on the regulatory context, performing demarcation whose direction is consistently self-serving. The dichotomy is not a pre-existing analytical category that platforms happen to fall between. It is being produced and maintained through specific legal and commercial practices.

Jasanoff’s idiom of co-production pushes this further. The platform’s technical architecture and its juridical identity are co-produced. The legal framework enables a particular technological design, and the technological design reinforces the plausibility of the legal claim. The effect is a systemic misrecognition in which algorithmic editorial power becomes invisible because the institutional apparatus classifies it as something else. The parallel to environmental governance is direct. When carbon footprint calculators individualise a structural problem, or when cost-benefit analysis translates incommensurable ecological loss into a commensurate metric, the same mechanism operates. A technical instrument produces a particular way of seeing that forecloses others, and the foreclosure is experienced as objectivity.

Cammaerts’ discussion of the GDPR crystallises this. He observes that Europe’s most robust privacy regulation amounts, in practice, to users consenting to their own surveillance. Refusal means exclusion from the service. The architecture of the consent interface enacts what Winner would recognise as politics embedded in technical design, where a structural power asymmetry is presented as individual choice. GY220 names this responsibilisation, the displacement of systemic accountability onto individual conduct. It is the same logic that underpins personal carbon footprint discourse and “media literacy” as the primary policy answer to platform harms. What STS adds is a vocabulary for understanding how it is technically accomplished, through material configurations that make one framing appear natural while rendering alternatives unthinkable.

Where the lecture left productive gaps was where Cammaerts’ normative commitments outpaced his analytical framework. His call for a “public service internet” is compelling as political aspiration. As a sociotechnical proposal, it remains underspecified. Jasanoff would ask what epistemic infrastructure such a project requires, whose expertise would be authoritative in its design, and how the forms of public participation governing its development might themselves reproduce existing power asymmetries. These are constitutive of whether the imaginary transforms or reproduces the dynamics Cammaerts critiques.

The deepest resonance between his project and GY220 may be methodological. Both arrive, from different disciplinary starting points, at the same conclusion. Binary oppositions are analytically generative when we refuse to resolve them. Cammaerts reaches this through critical political theory. STS reaches it through the empirical study of how knowledge and social order are mutually constituted. That convergence suggests that the instability of dichotomies is not a problem to be solved but a condition that reveals how power operates through the act of classification itself.

entry.title: Half-Past, or Thirty ‘Til
entry.content:
The past has no content – this is Allen’s claim and it is not a metaphor. Pastness is a position, not a warehouse of events that happened and were sealed but a place one occupies in relation to what has already been lost and what has not yet arrived, a place whose coordinates shift depending on where the body stands and what light happens to be falling on it (Allen, 2022, p. 1). I read this in the afternoon, sitting with There’s a Disco Ball Between Us, and I could parse it but I could not yet inhabit it. Inhabitation required something that came later, on a street that I had walked many times before and that would become unrecognisable.

Allen reimagines the Atlantic, the Middle Passage, the water that swallowed and carried and refused to return, as a collection of mirrors constantly reflecting and refracting, much like a disco ball (Allen, 2022, p. 3). Kevin Aviance, the performer, recalled looking into the disco ball at Club Palladium and seeing all his girlfriends who had died, their faces appearing inside the rotating mirrors, applauding slowly, and what was fucked up, he said, was that the number had gotten smaller because girls had gone on or died or passed on (Allen, 2022, p. 4). Allen does not treat this as grief-induced hallucination but as a practice of temporal habitation. The disco ball, by fragmenting light and refusing to let the room settle into a single stable image, produces the conditions under which coexistence with the dead becomes a sensory fact. Within Black gay time space, Allen writes, one can cut into the past and project a future in which we are still dancing with friends and lovers gone too soon, a temporality that is outside bourgeois time, outside nation time, ahead of time in culture, but also in many ways just out of time (Allen, 2022, p. 5). What makes the dance floor sacred is not the object that hangs from its ceiling but the density of what has been lived and lost beneath it.

I thought, reading this, of another story: a woman discovers a secret held by her twin sister and her mother, and they decide she cannot be allowed to keep it. They lure her to a dance hall called the Little Horse, a bribed bartender serves her a drugged drink, and in the confusion of the crowd the disco ball overhead – rigged, its mechanism filled with water – pours down and drowns her, there, under the lights, while the room keeps moving. The same object: in one narrative, the sanctuary where the dead return to the living; in another, the instrument of a murder that no one notices. The disco ball does not distinguish between these uses any more than the sea distinguishes between a ship and a body thrown from one. What makes a space sacred is thus the accumulation of what has been endured inside it, and by the same logic, what makes it lethal is the same indifference of the object to the bodies beneath it.

The lecture hall was warm and overlit, the opposite of the space I had been reading about. I sat near the back with a sheet of paper and a pen without laptop, because I wanted to watch the event whole.

Raewyn Connell stood up and I noticed, before anything she said, the body: broad shoulders, a visible Adam’s apple, and then a face that was entirely feminine in composition, the kind that in a photograph would register simply as a woman of a certain age. The voice carried a lower register that neither feminised itself nor asserted masculinity. With her mouth closed she was legible in one way; with it open she was legible in another; and the lag between these two readings was itself information, not about her but about the apparatus doing the reading, about how quickly and unconsciously perception sorts a body into a category and how disorienting it is when the sorting fails.

She said she had spent her whole life working towards this book and was the most reluctant to write it. Trans people, she said, are often required to explain themselves. The question she was interested in was not what it means to identify as a gender but who has access to that question at all, under what material conditions identification becomes possible, and what happens to those for whom the question never arises because they are too occupied with staying alive.

Connell has been dismantling sex role theory since the 1970s, the model in which there is a male role and a female role, learned through socialisation, enforced through sanctions. Her critique was that this picture erased power and economics from gender entirely, offering a world in which there were no structural victims, only well-socialised and badly-socialised subjects. What surprised her was that the same architecture reappeared in trans discourse in the 1990s, when the cisgender/transgender distinction became central. Cisgender people were the properly socialised and transgender people were the deviants. Ninety-nine per cent on one side, one per cent on the other. And the picture of the ninety-nine per cent was that gender had worked for them, that they had been smoothly installed into their roles, which was a claim so violently at odds with everything we know about the internal conflicts of gender conformity that she found it almost incredible it should have become the dominant framework. The line between cis and trans, she said, is a line you do not want to draw, because it erases what is shared, the collective experience of living in a gendered world, the tensions within so-called cisgender life, and replaces it with a division that serves no one, least of all those who need alliances most.

If the socialisation model is correct, then exclusion is a problem of individual formation rather than a problem of the system doing the forming. And what follows, if you happen to be someone whom the system has rendered unreadable, is not only the experience of being cast out but also the conviction that the casting out is deserved, that it reflects something deficient in you rather than something structural. The model lets you be expelled and feel guilty about the expulsion simultaneously, lets structural abandonment masquerade as personal failing, and its gravitational pull is so strong precisely because it speaks in the language of the self rather than the language of power.

Connell then reframed transition as joining, such as joining a community. She wanted to push against the radical individualism of rights-based trans politics, the model in which a single person claims recognition from the state and that transaction constitutes the horizon of liberation. Transition understood as joining implies solidarity and shared projects; trans groups are participating in changes that challenge mainstream power structures.

Joining, in the grammar of anti-trans rhetoric, becomes recruitment, and the recruitment narrative is old, reaching back through decades of homophobic imagery in which queer adults were figured as seducers and corrupters. We can break the contemporary contagion narrative into three registers: the psychological (the body-snatcher, the infiltrator who passes undetected), the religious (the demonic, the apocalyptic threat), and the public health register (the epidemic, the spreading pathology). What she insisted on was that the stakes are not evenly distributed: in places where life expectancy is already drastically shortened by structural deprivation, to playfully reclaim the language of contagion is not subversive but potentially catastrophic, because it hands the state a vocabulary the state has already shown it will use lethally. Every language of solidarity carries within it the blueprint for its weaponisation, and the problem is structural, as the same system that needs trans people to remain isolated will always re-read collective action as conspiracy.

Then Connell told a story. In Costa Rica, after a feminist conference, some young trans people had invited her for coffee, and at some point in the conversation the question arose: how long do we expect to live? They discussed it and arrived at a consensus of thirty-two. Connell realised she was already twice the age they expected to reach, and this is probably because of housing, disease, malnutrition, endemic violence. Rodriguez added another number, that Latina trans life expectancy in the United States is forty-four, a figure that does not appear in any nationalist metric of progress because it belongs to a population the national imaginary does not see.

Connell’s argument, stripped to its core, was that the real agenda for global trans politics must begin with survival, housing, nutrition, protection from violence, and that legal recognition and identity come after, because you must be permitted to live before you can contest the terms of your recognition. But the apparatus that must permit you to live is the same apparatus that has already decided who you are, and decided, in many cases, that who you are is not worth keeping alive. This does not resolve. It persists, and the fact that it persists while lectures are given and audiences applaud means only that these two temporalities – the temporality of intellectual reckoning and the temporality of early death – coexist without cancelling each other out, in much the same way that the disco ball holds the dead and the living in the same flicker without settling the difference between them.

The lecture ended and I walked out and the shift was immediate. Inside that room, for an hour and a half, the question of what gender is could be held open, transition was thinkable as a form of collective life rather than individual pathology, and an eighty-two-year-old woman with a man’s larynx could stand at a lectern and be entirely herself. The room had operated on folded time, past and present and future simultaneous, dense with the coexistence of multiple positions, refusing the linearity that would require each thing to stay in its place once it had happened.

Outside, the linearity reasserted itself at once. A couple on the pavement, holding hands, legible to the world in a way that required no effort. A mother and a small girl heading towards the theatre. A long queue of people waiting to see a play. All of it ordinary, all of it seamless, all of it operating below the threshold of what anyone there would call a system, you had to be standing outside it to see it as one, to notice that every body on that street had been assigned a position and was performing it with a fluency so total it had become indistinguishable from nature. I looked at these people and what I felt was not envy or anger but something closer to the vertigo of staring at a word until it stops looking like a word, until the letters separate and the meaning drains out and what remains is just marks on a surface, arbitrary, signifying only because everyone has agreed they do.

I thought: I am not a person, not in the way they are persons, not with that fluency, that ability to walk through the world and have the world confirm them at every step. However this is not self-pity since it requires a self that believes it deserves better. It is the experience of seeing the production line from outside, seeing how “person” is manufactured through a specific set of gendered, racialised, classed operations, and finding that you are not a product of that line and never were. In one sense this is a position of clarity, as you see the machinery because you are not inside it. But clarity is not the same as belonging, and you can understand a house perfectly and still have no key to its door.

I am twenty. Connell is eighty-two. The young people in Costa Rica expected thirty-two. Rodriguez cited forty-four. These are not data points but different durations of being permitted to exist, different lengths of time the system allocates before it withdraws its attention or intervenes to shorten what remains. Allen asks about the current moment – half-past, or thirty ‘til (Allen, 2022, p. 6) – and the question refuses to specify, because to specify would be to accept the clock being imposed: the clock that says childhood leads to adolescence leads to settling down, the clock under which deviance is a phase and desire eventually finds its proper reproductive form.

Pastness is a position. Passing is a position. Survival, for those whose expectancy has been compressed to thirty-two or forty-four, is a negotiation conducted within a system that has already decided the outcome. These three do not form a sequence. They coexist in the way that fragments of light coexist on the walls of a room with a disco ball turning in it, each catching a different angle, none producing a complete picture, all true at once, none true for long enough to hold. And perhaps what Allen means by thriving is the refusal to let the light fix you in one position, the insistence on continuing to turn even when the room was not built for you and the music was not chosen by you and the clock on the wall runs on someone else’s time, because to stop turning is to accept the linearity, and the linearity is what kills you, by deciding in advance how long you are allowed to move, and then calling the limit natural.

References

Allen, J. S. (2022). There’s a Disco Ball Between Us: A Theory of Black Gay Life. Duke University Press.

Connell, R. & Rodriguez, S. M. (2026). Trans Lives: Social Realities across the Globe. Public lecture, Department of Gender Studies, London School of Economics, 25 March.
entry.summary: The past has no content – this is Allen’s claim and it is not a metaphor. Pastness is a position, not a warehouse of events that happened

entry.title: Introducing "Best Before"
entry.content:
Update (2026-03-19): So I created another website called empIRe, since my friend said they wanted to have something similar for International Relations students as well.

So I built a supermarket.

Best Before is a website about expiration, of news, of attention, of knowledge, of the planet. It borrows the visual language of a grocery store. The Shelf pulls real-time environmental and climate news from RSS feeds (Mongabay, Grist, Global Voices, Yale E360, The Conversation), and presents them as reduced-to-clear products.

The Compost section is where things go to decompose into something useful. It is an environmental humanities resource hub organised as a supermarket floor plan. Each aisle holds a different category: academic papers and journals (auto-updating via RSS from Environmental Humanities, The Anthropocene Review, Cultural Geographies, Journal of Political Ecology), films, artworks and fashion, poetry and writing. There is also a Random Refresh aisle that gives you a writing prompt, a challenge, a fact, or a reading recommendation each time you visit, to learn whatever you land on.

Two other things are in Compost, which are adapted from my previous posts on May 3 and May 4 2025. The Anthropocene Calendar documents what happened on each calendar date during the Anthropocene, drawn from published sources across climate, ecology, and socio-technical history. And the Anthropocene Lottery is a lot-drawing ritual I wrote, with twenty possible endings for the human species, with one true ending. Some lines are adapted from the translated writings of Shi Tiesheng and it is not meant as prophecy.

The Label page is the back of the product. A single information sticker at the centre of a white page introducing this website.

The whole thing was built in a day with Lovable, with Claude handling the prompt engineering. The site’s favicon is a dandelion, a plant that looks like a flower but is usually pulled out as a weed, never allowed in the garden.
