entry.title: For All Women
entry.content:
Today is the eighth of March. It is also the ninth day of the war between the United States and Iran, in which at least 1,332 Iranian civilians have died so far, the majority of them in strikes on schools and hospitals.

The United Nations theme for this year’s International Women’s Day is “Rights, Justice, Action — for all women and girls.” The word all is doing a great deal of work here.

Earlier this week, I attended a webinar hosted by the Peace Economy Project, a fellowship programme I am part of as a decolonising research fellow, on the transfer of militarised frameworks from foreign policy into domestic governance. The panellists traced a consistent mechanism, that the label precedes the logic. Call someone a narco-terrorist, and the response is no longer law enforcement but warfare. Call protesters enemies from within, and the National Guard becomes a legitimate instrument of domestic order. The language, as one panellist put it, “accustoms people to think about martial responses to what are social problems.” What the label does, structurally, is remove the labelled person from the category of those who warrant protection, from due process and from the presumption of civilian status, and place them in the category of those against whom protection is exercised.

This is the mechanism the news cycle has been circling around today from several directions at once. In the United Kingdom, the Supreme Court ruled last year that transgender women do not fall within the legal definition of “woman” under the Equality Act, a decision whose consequences for trans people’s daily lives PinkNews has been documenting throughout. In the United States, three cases before the Supreme Court this year will determine whether conversion therapy bans violate free speech, whether trans girls can be excluded from women’s sport, and whether such exclusions breach the Fourteenth Amendment’s equal protection clause. In France, a coalition of feminist unions called today for a national strike, from work and from domestic labour, on the grounds that women still perform the majority of unpaid care while holding a fraction of legal and economic power. The UN puts the figure at 64% of men’s legal rights globally.

These share a structural logic, that protection of a defined category requires the prior act of defining who falls within it, and that act of definition is never politically neutral. The border of all women is not a natural perimeter and it is in fact drawn and contested.

What the PEP webinar made clear is that this drawing of borders accelerates under militarised conditions. When emergency powers are declared or the insurrection Act is invoked, the institutions that normally adjudicate who belongs where are progressively sidelined. One of the panellists noted that since 1979 there has been an uninterrupted national emergency regarding Iran still technically on the books; that emergency powers, once activated, almost never fully expire; and that the courts have historically been deferential to the executive on anything framed in terms of national security. The emergency state does not suspend the question of who counts. It just answers it faster, with less deliberation, and in favour of whoever currently holds the power to answer.

Each case here shares a similar position, that each is subject to a system that defines the scope of its own protection, and each falls, in different ways and to different degrees, outside the line that system has drawn. What the International Women‘s Day cannot do, from within its own framework, is resolve the tension between all as aspiration and all as the thing that keeps being renegotiated. That tension is the actual political condition the occasion is marking.

entry.title: On Violence and Its Frames
entry.content:
“Boy you don’t understand wude (小伙子你不讲武德).” — Ma Baoguo (马保国)

In May 2020, the self-styled grandmaster of “Hunyuan Xinyi Taiji”, a form of traditional Chinese kung fu he claimed could neutralise opponents twice his size, was knocked down three times in thirty seconds by an amateur martial artist in his late forties. The footage went viral and what followed was a reframe, stating that the young man had launched a surprise attack at the moment of Ma’s deliberate restraint, violating wude, the ethical code of the fighter. Ma had placed his fist near the young man’s nose without striking, “point to stop, as traditional kung fu demands (传统功夫以点到为止),” and been repaid with a punch to the eye. The loss, by this account, was not a loss at all but evidence of the opponent’s unworthiness.

The move is precise enough to be worth examining. By first establishing the norm that traditional kung fu operates through restraint, Ma changes defeat into moral vindication. Violence that works against one becomes proof of the other’s bad faith; violence one claim to have withheld becomes proof of mastery.

This is the structure of a particular kind of argument about violence: that it works, that the capacity for it is what ultimately determines outcomes, and that failures can always be attributed to rule-breaking rather than to any inadequacy in the premise. The argument is circular in a way that looks like evidence. Because the belief that violence is effective produces a disposition toward violent resolution, and violent resolution, when it works, confirms the belief, the loop closes without ever needing to test itself against a genuine counterexample. Benjamin‘s distinction between law-making and law-preserving violence captures something of this, that violence does not just disrupt order, it constitutes the order that in turn keeps producing the conditions under which violence looks necessary.

Whether this logic is specifically masculine is a question worth pausing on, not least because the answer is less obvious than it appears. The association between violence and masculine identity is real and well-documented, but “violence as the final arbiter of power” operates just as readily at the level of the state, the colonial administration, the development agency. Fanon‘s account of colonial violence, in which the colonised subject can only reclaim subjecthood through force, because every other avenue of self-assertion has been foreclosed, suggests that the relationship between violence and masculinity is situational. It is what happens when the capacity for violence becomes the only currency that the existing order will recognise. The question thus shifts from “is this masculine” to “what conditions make violence the only legible proof of power.”

Shrey Kapoor put pressure on this question in the Human Geography seminar this week, tracing the relationship between communal violence and urban development in Ahmedabad across the long twentieth century. His argument, compressed that anti-Muslim violence in Modi’s Gujarat was never only destructive. It was constitutive as it forged Hindu unity across caste lines, hardened the communal frontiers that became material walls, and produced the segregated spatial order that Hindu nationalist hegemony required as its operating environment. After the 2002 pogrom killed close to a thousand people, mostly Muslim, the visibility of state-backed violence became a liability. Investor anxiety and international visa bans showed that the violence had consolidated power but also revealed the fragility of the project. Modi’s response was to sublimate it. The Sabarmati Riverfront Project, relaunched under his direct control in 2003, displaced over 40,000 lower-caste Hindu and Muslim labourers who had lived on the riverbanks for generations. The evictions were framed as urban renewal. Thus the displaced became encroachers and their removal became progress.

Kapoor calls this communal capitalism, borrowing the logic of racial capitalism to argue that capital accumulation and communal violence are not parallel processes but the same process, where capitalist instruments serve communal ends and the violence of dispossession is rendered legible as development. The displaced populations, who had been the targets of riot violence for decades, became the targets of infrastructural dispossession, with the crucial difference that the removal now had a planning document behind it.

This is where the definition of violence starts to matter, and where a certain intellectual honesty is required. There is a legitimate objection to the way “violence” has expanded in recent decades such as “slow violence”, “symbolic violence”, “bureaucratic violence”, until it threatens to become a catch-all term that describes everything, in much the same way that “decolonisation” risks losing its analytical edge when applied metaphorically. If violence means a punch to the face and also means a planning document and also means a street renaming, the concept may be doing too much work, and the specificity of each form of harm gets flattened in the process.

Kapoor does not entirely escape this tension, but what makes his account more careful than the generic “development-as-violence” argument is that he traces the material connection between the two registers rather than simply asserting their equivalence. With the same populations and the same political project, riot violence and infrastructural dispossession were sequential operations, where the first created the conditions, eroding intercommunal trust, fracturing the local brokerage networks that had sustained mixed settlement, that made the second possible. Here the bureaucratic procedure was not a metaphor for violence. It was violence organised differently, requiring the prior violence to function.

Butler‘s analysis of frames of war becomes useful here, though again with some caution about what the framework is actually claiming. The point is not that all framings are equally arbitrary, but that the question of whose violence counts as violence, and whose counts as self-defence, or development, or the restoration of order, is never settled by the act itself. Ma Baoguo did not lose a fight and then describe it accurately. He lost a fight and then described it in a way that redistributed culpability. The woman in Kapoor’s account who sold her deed to a resettlement unit after being told that Muslims in the adjacent yard were throwing stones at Hindu residents (only to discover later that it was the community broker’s own entourage doing the throwing) was not deceived about a fact. She was deceived about the frame. The broker had manufactured the fear that made his services necessary, and the fear was real enough to act on regardless of its origin.

What this produces, taken together, is not quite the argument that violence always wins or that moral reasoning is merely decorative. It is in fact about the capacity to determine what counts as violence, and therefore what counts as legitimate response, is itself a form of power, and one that tends to accrue to whoever already controls the material conditions under which both the violence and its description occur. Ma Baoguo lost the fight. He has not, in any obvious sense, lost the argument about who didn’t observe wude. Whether that distinction matters depends on what one think the argument was ever about.

entry.title: Constructing Humanity:On The Politics of World Heritage
entry.content:
On the fourth of March, the LSE Department of International Relations hosted a book launch for Elif Kalaycioglu’s The Politics of World Heritage: Visions, Custodians, and Futures of Humanity, published by Oxford University Press. Kalaycioglu is a lecturer at King’s College London, and the book draws on decades of archival research and fieldwork within the UNESCO World Heritage regime, the institutional machinery that decides, since 1972, which sites belong to humanity.

The opening problem the book poses is deceptively simple. The World Heritage Convention asserts that certain places in the world are of such outstanding interest that they must be preserved as part of the heritage of mankind as a whole. But mankind, as a cultural and historical subject with a shared memory, does not exist prior to that assertion. It has to be made. Kalaycioglu’s argument is that the regime has been making it and remaking it for over fifty years, and that the social and political orders which emerge from those constructions are neither neutral nor stable.

The analysis moves through three periods, each organised around a distinct vision of humanity. In the regime’s early decades, humanity was conceived as a rarefied, transhistorical subject: the depositary of the highest forms of human creativity and aesthetic genius. The criteria for outstanding universal value, formulated by ICOMOS in 1976 and shaped almost entirely by Western European and North American experts, valorised monumentality, grand civilisational artefacts, urban planning, and the progressive arc of world history. The heritage list that emerged from these criteria was, predictably, a map of a humanity whose long stay and centre of gravity was in Europe. Colonial cities in South America were praised as demonstrations of ingenuity in the adoption of universal principles to local conditions, a framing that made post-colonial states’ claims to heritage legible only through the terms of the very history that had dispossessed them. A handwritten note from UNESCO’s then Director-General Amadou-Mahtar M’Bow, attached to an internally circulated memo, urged that the evaluation criteria not be established on the basis of cultural designs valid only for part of the world. That call went unheeded.

The second period brought a paradigm shift, driven by a subgroup of experts, anthropologists, and Australian and New Zealand specialists who had been working through domestic contestations around indigenous heritage, who introduced new resources into the regime’s symbolic universe about vernacular architecture, know-how, living cultures, harmonious human-nature relations. The vision of humanity shifted from the rarefied to the diverse. Sites previously rejected or invisible became legible. Zanzibar, once dismissed for preserving only recent vestiges of its history, was reinscribed as demonstrating an outstanding fusion of cultures. Indigenous sites in Australia and New Zealand, previously recognised only as natural heritage, acquired cultural value. The shift was, on the whole, a positive development, but it arrived with its own hierarchies. An early workshop organised for African experts illustrates the tension. One European expert praised the turn toward anthropological parameters as finally allowing African heritage to be represented on its own terms; another described that same heritage, in the same meeting, as possessing the haunting charm of human being at its prime, the language of appreciation that carries the logic of primitivism.

The third period, from around 2010, brought a different kind of assertion. States began positioning themselves as the proper adjudicators, contributors, and custodians of world heritage, and through it humanity. Expert evaluations were increasingly overturned at committee meetings. The vision of a diverse humanity was retained, but firmly attached to the nation-state as its natural representative, diversity as the sum of sovereign parts. China’s revitalisation of the Silk Roads heritage, tightly tethered to the Belt and Road Initiative within the regime’s symbolic universe, is the clearest example. It is a world-historical narrative of peaceful trade and exchange, through which China positions itself as a subject that has steered a diverse humanity’s global relations before and can do so again. The irony Kalaycioglu identifies is structural. In their pursuit of the prestige that world heritage confers, a prestige grounded precisely in the more-than-national character of outstanding universal value, states risk collapsing the very distinction that generates the prestige. If humanity is the aggregate of nation-states, adjudicated by states as such, heritage can never be more than an internationally endorsed national honour roll.

What keeps the regime from fully dissolving into that contradiction, Kalaycioglu suggests, is that states continue to employ the symbolic resources of the convention even as they assert their sovereign prerogatives. They know, as she puts it, that they are breaking the toy and that they should not break it entirely if they want to keep playing with it. Peace and solidarity remain in circulation as legitimising frames, even under conditions of increasing state centrism. The nomination file for the Bikini Atoll Nuclear Test Site, submitted by the Republic of Marshall Islands, offers what Kalaycioglu calls a nested and uneven construction of humanity, one that holds together the global significance of nuclear weapons technology with the radically unequal distribution of their consequences across populations. It does not dispense with the universality, but it does not flatten the hierarchy either. Whether this kind of construction can do more political work than the regime’s dominant modes remains, at the end of the book, an open question.

The discussion that followed the presentation circled back repeatedly to the problem of adjudication, about how outstanding universal value can be determined at all once the symbolic universe has been expanded to include vernacular and living cultures, which resist the traceable monumentality that made the original criteria legible. Kalaycioglu’s answer was: the expert reports have become more scientifically elaborate precisely to speak to an uncertainty they cannot resolve. The aspiration and the method are not, at this point, hanging neatly together. The regime continues to function, and the list continues to grow, but what it is doing and for whom, remains a question the institution is not well-positioned to answer from inside itself.

entry.title: The Invisible Heart:On the Care Economy and Social Housing
entry.content:
On the third of March, LSE Housing and Communities hosted a public panel on the relationship between the care economy and social housing, featuring Anne Power, emeritus professor of social policy at LSE and author of Beyond Bricks and Mortar; Tim Jackson, ecological economist at the University of Surrey and author of The Care Economy; and Jonathon Porritt, writer and long-time campaigner on sustainable development. The three panellists had sat together on the UK Sustainable Development Commission for nearly a decade, which is a shared history that gave the conversation an unusual density of reference, and an occasional candour about the limits of what they had managed to achieve.

Anne Power opened with a deceptively simple claim that social housing is not just an instance of the care economy but one of its clearest illustrations. The argument moves through history. From medieval almshouses, of which around three thousand survive in England today, and whose residents live on average two years longer than the general population, not despite their age and poverty but, Power argues, because of the quality of care organised around them, through Robert Owen’s New Lanark, Octavia Hill’s tenant management experiments, the Quaker industrial villages, and the Peabody Trust, a consistent logic appears. Housing that works is housing that is maintained and embedded in a community structure that takes ongoing responsibility for both the physical fabric and the people within it. The nineteenth-century models, for all their paternalism, understood this. The twentieth-century state, in Power’s telling, largely forgot it. Between the wars and through to 1980, sixty-five million council homes were built, a third of total stock, by administrations too preoccupied with construction targets to attend to management. As the most disadvantaged households were concentrated into the newest and least desirable estates, council housing became what planners called difficult to let. The housing associations that had operated alongside councils, small and community-rooted, were then drawn into the same logic, that pressured to absorb large-scale stock transfers, forced to borrow from private markets, they became developers, and the caring economy came into conflict with itself.

Tim Jackson’s contribution took the argument to a different register. His guiding question, “what can prosperity possibly mean on a finite planet,” reframes the problem entirely. The conventional answer, that prosperity is wealth and wealth is accumulation, breaks down not only under ecological constraints but under its own internal contradictions. When Jackson asked people directly what prosperity meant to them, health came out at or near the top. Health of self, family, community, environment. What would follow, he asked, if we took that seriously, if we organised the economy around health rather than wealth? The analogy he reaches for is physiological, a slow breath rather than hyperventilation. Care, in this frame is, as the sociologist Joan Tronto put it, everything we do to maintain or repair our world so that we can live in it as well as possible. It lies at what Nancy Folbre calls the invisible heart of the economy, that without it, there is no economy at the most basic level, yet it is systematically undervalued and feminised. The employment-intensive sectors closest to care have the lowest material and environmental footprints. They represent, Jackson argues, a kind of economic sweet spot, a blueprint for a wellbeing economy. Care’s virtues are capitalism’s vices. Employment intensity reads, in mainstream economics, as low productivity growth. Wages follow productivity, so care workers are condemned to precarious conditions and low status, while the extractive logic of financialisation strips value from the sectors care depends on.

Porritt brought the ideological genealogy. The care deficit, he argued, did not accumulate by accident or through a sequence of bad decisions. Its roots lie in the Mont Pelerin Society, founded in 1947, and the slow maturation of neoliberal ideas through the 1950s and 1960s until the moment, around 1979, when they became policy. Three mechanisms in particular: the progressive marketisation of the state at every level; the licensed externalisation of costs from private balance sheets onto society; and the financialisation of the economy, whose consequences in the care sector are now visible in the figures for children in care, cost per child rising from £160,000 to £320,000 per annum over twenty years, driven not by better outcomes but by debt servicing, executive bonuses, and the architecture of private finance. Porritt was more direct than the others about what this represents.

The discussion that followed circled around two questions the panellists could not quite resolve. The first was historical: when, if ever, had a British government genuinely placed care at the centre of its politics? The answers offered, Clement Attlee, perhaps the early years of New Labour, perhaps neither, suggested more about the limits of the political imagination than about any recoverable tradition. The second was structural: whether a single country could transition toward a care-oriented economy within a global system still organised around extractive growth. Jackson’s position was cautious but not entirely pessimistic: care is typically local and non-traded, which means it can be nurtured locally even under adverse international conditions. Porritt was less sanguine, the analogy to climate action held, he thought, and the conclusion was similar: you cannot decouple unilaterally from a system whose logic pervades every level of governance and finance.

What remained unresolved at the end of the evening was the question of mechanism. The diagnosis that the logic of accumulation destroys the logic of care, that housing becomes dysfunctional when it becomes an asset class, that care workers are structurally condemned to bad conditions by a productivity metric rigged against them, was stated clearly and from multiple directions. What a transition toward something different would actually require, whether in housing policy, in care sector regulation, or in the deeper architecture of how the economy values work, was gestured at rather than answered.

entry.title: What Does it Mean to Be in the Wrong Body?
entry.content:
“we were never meant to survive.” — Audre Lorde, cited in Munhazim & Zondon (2021)

That day the rain fell without pause (1). Inside, the air was damp and stifling; the servants had wrung their palms damp against the corners of their robes. The smell of blood saturated everything, but the windows were shut against the rain and the cold. The wooden furniture swayed alongside Wujiang, daughter of the Lord of Shen, brow locked tight, wood-brown and blood-red and the white of rain heard from the deep of her ears tangling and overlapping in her field of vision, a sudden dizziness sweeping through her.

The midwife wrenched the infant out by its feet. Yes, feet first. Wujiang’s hatred was complete. Even in her exhaustion she moved her eyes to that wrinkled face. Ugly, and she had nearly died for this. Not dead, but half her life gone with it.

The massive haemorrhage of a difficult birth let Wujiang channel every bone-deep pain into hatred, branding a red scar in her heart for that unworthy child.

The experienced midwife took up the scalding silver scissors and cut the umbilical cord without hesitation. The crisp snap was slightly piercing. Wujiang felt some emotion inside her shatter with it. This cut, had severed the bond between mother and son for good.

The infant’s crying made the night long. It mixed with the nauseating, suffocating smell of blood, and the endless, monotonous, drumbeat rain.

Wujiang raised a finger toward the newborn. The Lord of Zheng, just entering, stepped forward and tilted his head. For one moment he caught sight of a surging malice flaring in the rims of Wujiang’s reddened eyes, something beyond the flowing tears and demanded attention.

But the joy of a newborn clouded the Lord of Zheng’s mind. He gathered the child into his arms and forgot to take Wujiang’s outstretched hand.

“Call him Wusheng…”

Her last thread of vision fixed on the floor, where blood ran freely, the Lord of Zheng standing in exactly that position, his child in his arms. Hatred and warmth went cold together, folding inward as her eyes closed.

Wusheng: in that era, a byword for a child born in difficult labour. Every time Wujiang saw him, the name would drag tonight’s pain and fright back to the surface, and all of Zheng would know that their future ruler had come into the world the wrong way.

Is this repugnant? A figure leans toward Mulan (2). What do you think? From Mencius’s mother moving house three times to the weeping of Youzi Yin, the stories of maternal devotion that circulate as cultural bedrock are well known. But Wujiang escapes that script entirely. Because the birth made her suffer, she hated the child, named him after her own agony. Yet it is also, somehow, not incomprehensible. The pain was real. The child was hers; she could name him whatever she liked. And as Schneider observed, blood is ultimately just a fluid; there is nothing inside it that naturally produces ties that are deep and strong (2004, p. 268).

Mulan understands this because she has lived the corollary. Conscripted into her father’s place, she shed her women’s clothes and went to war, and became a general. For years she moved inside a world that had never been built for her. When the war ended she stood before the emperor and made the argument that a woman, too, can do this. The emperor had her executed for the deception. She laughed absurdly, because she had always suspected it would come to this. That the achievement would dissolve the moment the body behind it was named. On her deathbed she says: next life, I want to be a man. Next life, a man. As a child, her grandmother had looked at her and said: what a pity, not a boy. Now she looks at her own child and says the same. The wrong body, in Mulan’s case, is not hers, it is the world’s.

This distinction matters. Contemporary transgender discourse rests on a claim about interiority that gender identity is a prior truth which the body either confirms or fails to express, that the self knows something the anatomy does not. This writing does not dispute the reality of that experience. It asks, instead, what kind of claim it is: whether the wrong-body narrative describes a universal condition of gender variance, or whether it is a historically specific and culturally particular translation of something more diffuse, a language developed to address certain institutions, which has become the only available grammar for experiences that exceed it.

I. The Constructionist Premise and Its Internal Pressure

The argument that gender is socially constructed has become axiomatic in feminist anthropology since Collier and Yanagisako’s insistence on “calling into question the universality of our cultural assumptions about the difference between males and females” (1994, p. 199). Schneider extended the logic further. Kinship — the grid through which biological relatedness had been naturalised as social bedrock — was an analytic category with “no discernible cultural referent in fact” (2004, p. 269). Meaning reaches backwards and selectively illuminates biology, and biology does not generate meaning on its own.

Transgender theory inherits this critique. If gender roles and gendered embodiment are cultural productions, then assignment at birth on the basis of anatomy is exactly the naturalisation that critical theory exists to dismantle. The category of transgender travels across cultural contexts, but in travelling it reshapes what it purports only to describe. Importing, as it moves, is a specific epistemological architecture in which gender variance is authorised through psychological interiority rather than through kinship or ritual function.

The difficulty emerges when the experiential claims of transgender identity are placed back against this theoretical premise. To say “I am a woman despite being assigned male at birth” is a rejection of biological determinism, but embedded within that rejection is an inner sense of gender that the social world has failed to recognise. This is not only a phenomenological claim about distress but an ontological claim about what one is, prior to and in excess of social inscription. The tension runs through the conceptual architecture of transgender discourse itself. It simultaneously dismantles gender as natural and reinstates it as inner truth. The wrong-body narrative relocates essentialism, moving it from anatomy to psychology while leaving the structure intact.

II. The Body That Knows

Blackwood’s account of tombois in West Sumatra shows how “culturally coded categories shape, inflect, and infuse gender identities” through an ongoing social process in which individuals “negotiate, stabilise a sense of who they are” in relation to dominant gender ideologies (1998, p. 492). The tomboi identity is produced through specific material practices and relational contexts, yet the women Blackwood describes experience their identities as irreducibly their own, resistant to the cewek role others attempt to impose. Thus cultural mediation and felt authenticity are not opposites. The constructionist account explains the mechanism without dissolving the phenomenological weight.

The Mojave cases in Living the Spirit (1988) push this further. The alyha and hwame roles were predestined by dreams, arriving through a cultural mechanism that positioned them as given, fated, ontologically prior to individual volition. Here the wrong-body narrative appears in a different idiom entirely. Not that “my psychology contradicts my anatomy,” but “the dream spoke before the body was fixed.” The ontological claim is equally strong, but it is authorised through cosmology. This shows that the claim that gender identity exceeds social assignment is not unique to Western transgender discourse, however the epistemological register in which that excess is authorised varies so radically across contexts that treating them as instances of the same phenomenon obscures more than it reveals. The wrong body therefore is a culturally specific translation of something more diffuse, one that makes sense within a medical and legal system organised around psychological interiority, and becomes available as a script only to those whom that system can hear.

III. Disidentification and the Limits of Legibility

Muñoz’s concept of disidentification offers a way to hold this complexity. Neither identification with a dominant category nor its outright rejection, disidentification is a working on and against simultaneously, “an intersectional strategy” that registers subjects as “constructed and contradictory” (1997, p. 84). Identity categories, including “transgender,” are reworked through inhabitation, and the reworking leaves traces that exceed the category’s original design. The question is what the wrong-body narrative does: what it makes possible, what it forecloses, and for whom it functions as an available script.

The narrative is not equally accessible to all trans subjects. It emerged from and continues to circulate most powerfully within a white, Western, medicalised context where psychological interiority is the dominant mode of authorising identity claims. The queer Muslim subjects in Munhazim and Zondon’s autoethnography articulate their experience in an entirely different register, as lives structured by the proximity of death, by “living deaths” and “unlived desires” that accumulate in the absence of any legitimate space for self-expression (2021). One of them describes the experience of hearing his father wish him dead at twenty-one: “I felt life exiting my body and leaving the room through the cracks of the window and into the breeze outside. It felt what Eric Stanley calls ‘death-in-waiting’” (Munhazim & Zondon, 2021). What he inhabits is instead a condition of social erasure, of being alive but unrecognised, present but expelled. The wrong-body narrative is not his narrative. The institutions that narrative addresses are not the institutions that govern his life.

The script’s coherence depends on a set of legal and medical apparatuses that presuppose a subject capable of making rights claims, a presupposition that structurally excludes those who have already been expelled from recognition entirely.

IV. Kinship, Care, and the Relational Alternative

Borneman’s argument is that anthropology has consistently privileged “forms of communal reproduction” over “processes of voluntary affiliation: processes of caring and being cared for” (1997, p. 574). The case he offers was about a man named Dieter who formed a bond with Harald, his mother’s former lover, a relationship that was “neither articulable nor re-presentable in anthropological categories, yet it was significant and above all, it was fundamentally human” (1997, p. 581). What made it real was the mutual care that constituted it over time. The bond could not be named but existed anyway, in the texture of specific dependencies and specific forms of being-held. “Care is the source and result of human creativity,” Borneman concludes: “We should recognise it as such” (1997, p. 583).

Transposing this logic to gender identity does not require abandoning the phenomenological reality of trans experience. If identity is an ongoing process of negotiation and stabilisation (Blackwood, 1998, p. 492), and if belonging is constituted through care rather than prior essence (Borneman, 1997), then “being a woman” need not be understood as a pre-social fact awaiting discovery, nor reduced to performance alone. It is produced through the specific ways a person is cared for and cares for others. The wrong-body narrative, on this reading, articulates that the experience of being constituted in one relational register while remaining legible to institutions only in another. Therefore, the disjunction here is between how one is held in relation and how one is classified by power, instead of being between an inner truth and its outer misrepresentation.

V. The Transitional Language Hypothesis

Benjamin’s argument that “racist structures not only produce, but reproduce whiteness” through systems that are “thereby reproductive systems” (2018, p. 43) carries a structural logic portable to gender. The categories that produce legible femininity and masculinity are themselves reproductive, as they generate the conditions under which certain gender experiences become recognisable as authentic and others remain unreadable. The wrong-body narrative is, among other things, a strategy for becoming legible within a medical and legal system that requires a coherent account of gender misalignment to authorise transition, a form of address directed at institutions that can only hear the language of inner truth and bodily evidence.

The distress this narrative describes is real. Munhazim and Zondon’s account of living as “the undead: even if we were to live beyond 25, we would compromise our living by killing off dreams of a fully self-expressed existence” (2021) is testimony. The strongest rebuttal to this essay’s argument insists exactly on this: the care-based relational framework, however theoretically elegant, offers nothing operable to a person whose legal documents do not match their body, whose safety depends on institutional recognition, whose survival requires the wrong-body narrative to work. That pressure is real and should not be dismissed.

But the narrative’s institutional utility deepens its theoretical instability. Every time the wrong-body narrative successfully secures legal recognition or medical access, the institutions that granted that recognition are reinforced in their demand for it. The narrative becomes harder to replace, not easier. A language developed to address one set of institutions may gradually become the only available grammar for experiences that exceed it, and in that process, the winkte, the alyha, the tomboi, the queer Afghan subject are foreclosed, their ways of inhabiting gender rendered illegible by the very framework that claims to liberate gender from biology. The wrong-body narrative’s success is also, structurally, its reproduction of the binary it set out to dismantle. This is not an argument against transition, or against the protections the narrative has secured. It is an observation about what kind of thing the narrative is. It is a historically conditioned and institutionally dependent translation strategy, one that in working, narrows what can be said.

Conclusion

Collier asks: “What we can begin to ask is what we want our families to do” (1997, p. 80). The same question can be directed at gender categories. The wrong-body narrative has done political work that cannot be dismissed. It has secured legal recognition and medical access for people whose lives would otherwise be entirely unreadable to the institutions that govern them. But as an account of what gender is, of what the world consists of, to return to Schneider’s question, it reinstates a metaphysics of inner essence that constructionism spent decades dismantling, and it does so in a way that reproduces the binary it claims to transcend.

There is a world I find myself imagining, one in which people look at each other and see only the irreducible particularity of a soul, in which what a person is cannot be read off the surface of a body or confirmed by a document. In that world, care, not anatomy, would be the ground of recognition. Borneman’s formulation would hold: “Care is the source and result of human creativity. We should recognise it as such” (1997, p. 583).

But the question that stays with me is this: if we arrived at that world, would the concept of transgender still need to exist? Is it a name for something permanent in human experience, a mode of being that would persist even in the absence of binary gender norms, or is it a tool developed for navigating a particular historical arrangement, necessary just because that arrangement has not yet ended? I do not know. The winkte was given a name by a cosmology that no longer governs the world it once organised. The tomboi negotiates a gender ideology that is itself in flux. Mulan laughed on her deathbed because she understood that the system would not be moved. What I cannot determine is whether the wrong-body narrative is the laugh, or the system.

Notes

1: Zheng Bo Ke Duan Yu Yan (郑伯克段于鄢) is a narrative from the Zuo Zhuan (左传), a chronicle of the Spring and Autumn period (771–476 BCE). The passage above is a fictional reconstruction of the circumstances surrounding the birth of Zhuang Gong of Zheng, born feet-first, an event that, according to the Zuo Zhuan, caused his mother Wujiang to resent him from birth. The name she gave him, Wusheng (寤生), carried the meaning of a child born in difficult labour, and functioned as a public record of her suffering written into his identity.

2: Mulan is a fictional character whose origin lies in the Ballad of Mulan (木兰辞, c. 5th–6th century CE), the anonymous Northern Wei poem in which a woman disguises herself as a man to take her ageing father’s place in military conscription. The version of Mulan referred to here departs from the ballad: she does not return safely home, and the emperor does not reward her. Her story is used here as a thought experiment about the structural conditions under which gender variance becomes a survival strategy rather than an identity claim.

3: This writing was written after a week of self-directed reading from the AN488 Gender, Sexuality and Kinship course reading list. I have not formally taken the course. As such, this piece should be read as a provisional exploration rather than a fully informed anthropological argument. Any misunderstandings or oversimplifications are entirely my own.

entry.title: Filth Commons
entry.content:
I have lost, in one way or another, the vitality to write.

In the gaps between stations, not a single moving sentence came to me. I stood watching for a long while as children ran in the distance, tripping over each other, and a golden retriever bounced back and forth like an enchanted scarecrow taking flight. A seagull swept past like a warship crossing a grassland as vast as a sixth ocean.

It suddenly occurred to me that I don’t like using personal pronouns. Because to be “in the Filth Commons” means we no longer meet the administrative definition of “the livings.” We are objects outside the subject-body of domestic residents, of one substance with waste. Of one substance with the seagull, of one substance with the grassland. Identity is fluid or has been stripped away, so our sentences usually carry no first-person subject. We are together. I am nothing more than one eye in the body that is the Filth Commons; the seagull is a little finger; the grassland is a patch of skin.

My physical death is only a temporary blindness of ours. The seagull’s death is only a brief spasm in a little finger. Each fulfilling a role while alive, none knowing the other, yet all housed within the same body. We constitute the body, but the body sustains no great loss when it loses us.

Outside last night’s guesthouse stood a mask, resembling the classic demon figures from home, yet belonging to some distant religious ritual. The host’s skin was a dark green, faintly exuding the smell of chemicals. A diffuser sat in the room; I couldn’t sleep. The door had no keyhole. At any moment a silhouette might appear against the translucent window. Another set of blinds kept flaring up suddenly, disturbed by the motion-sensor light as pedestrians passed. At dinnertime, that child cried a lot. The hostress had her heavy back turned to me as I left. I wandered through the darkened streets, only a cat darting past the stalled cars. Then back again, to this house at the end of the road.

This morning I finally caught sight of the hostress. She returned my greeting with a worn-out look and hurried past. Will my future be the same, eking out an existence in some corner of the Filth Commons? Forced to rent out part of the house as a cheap guesthouse, strangers endlessly entering the private home, the child always crying. Yet the home itself always frightfully quiet. Oh, home comes from far away. They say some marginalized groups have already “erupted in silence,” but we cannot feel it. Love and violence alike arrive slowly.

entry.title: On Editing a Journal
entry.content:
On the evening of February 16th, I finished editing the 4th volume of the LSE journal of Geography and Environment.

Three months. When I try to look back, the details have already thinned, compressed by time into shapes, then into light. What remains are flashes. And underneath it all, something more persistent, gratitude, and a love for the work itself.

My dashboard has carried a line for a long time: “God’s mercy is that wherever you wish to go, a road will appear.” A friend who has given me much support has something similar: “as long as I wish to walk, there will be a road for me to step on.” One leans toward fate; the other toward will. But I find them meeting at the same point. And this is also, I think, what the journal is about:

At its core, JGE exists to gather diverse perspectives, theories, and contexts into one collective work, freely accessible and open to all. Each article brings its own colour, each perspective its own brushstroke, and together, they compose a vivid picture of what geography means to this generation of students.

That kind of colour lit my way through editing.

The first time I saw the journal’s website, I decided immediately that I want to be the next editor. Or at least do UI design for the editorial team. I had the feeling before I had the words for it. Later I applied for the URF fellowship, and became sub-editor.

The editorial team was just Tom and me. He gave me an enormous amount of freedom, and I loved his way of working, open trust, and the kind of autonomy that makes creativity feel possible rather than permitted. I came out of every meeting feeling energised.

So I tried everything, all at once, because this was also my first time.

Redesigning the website interface and icons. Rewriting the About page. Coordinating with department staff, who were, without exception, genuinely kind. Setting deadlines. Inviting authors. Opening the first submission portal. Reviewing manuscripts. Copyediting. Designing five A1 exhibition boards. Laying out a booklet, a poster, a leaflet. Designing the cover and back cover. Writing the acknowledgements.

At the end of it, I looked at what I’d done and felt something like surprise. I’d moved between design, communication, and writing simultaneously for months. Apparently I could do that, and apparently I liked it.

Outside of coursework and research, to have this kind of fellowship was a privilege. It felt like stepping back from being a researcher and becoming, instead, someone who weaves research together, like curating, or playing a game of chess with no opponent. The board was intricate and the moves kept branching.

Or maybe it was more like designing a device. One that resembles a garden, a garment, a book, a piece of music, I can’t quite fix on one. It has documents that carry the names of those who came before. It has present authors and supporters. It has future readers. Its dimension exceeds three, because it points simultaneously to past, present, and future. It has the force of a collective, writers of different backgrounds, nationalities, disciplines, all appearing in the same space, each on equal footing.

In the acknowledgements, I wrote we. The editorial team was, in practice, Tom and me. But the we felt right and it still does.

There are things I’d have done differently. A few articles I very much wanted to include couldn’t be, for various reasons. Citation formatting was imperfect as I didn’t have the bandwidth to catch everything. There was no second pair of eyes; I am not a native English speaker; I accept that there are small errors I’ll never find.

When I first took this on, the journal was like cloth full of holes. I should say clearly that I am grateful to the editors before me, reading through past volumes while working on this one, I learned from them too. What I built, I built on something.

I can’t say everything.

Thank you to everyone who accompanied and supported this, across the whole stretch of it. This is a collective road, made of past, present, and future, of us and you and them. What Volume 4 records, Volume 5 will continue, from a new angle, in a new voice.

From nothing to something.

From 2025 to 2026.

Happy New Year.

entry.title: Can Natural Capital Be Replaced? Notes from Eric Neumayer's Lecture
entry.content:
On 10 February, the LSE Department of Geography and Environment, together with the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment and the LSE Sustainability Initiative, hosted a public lecture by Professor Eric Neumayer to mark the open-access publication of the fifth edition of his book, Weak versus Strong Sustainability, first published in 1999. The event was held at the Shaw Theatre and chaired by Professor Hyun Bang Shin. What follows is a summary of the lecture, with connections drawn to the core concepts covered in GY222 (Applied Environmental Economics).

Every 90 minutes, around seven million tonnes of CO₂ are emitted, approximately 1,000 football pitches of primary tropical rainforest disappear, somewhere between one and seven species go extinct, and roughly 1,400 people die from air pollution-related illness. These figures, Prof. Neumayer argued, frame the central question of his life’s work: does any of this actually matter, from an economic standpoint? The answer turns out depending entirely on which theory of sustainability one adopts.

The I=PAT Framework and What It Misses

Students of GY222 will recognise the I=PAT identity (Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology) as a diagnostic tool for breaking down the sources of environmental pressure. Neumayer’s lecture implicitly engages with the “A” and “T” terms throughout: the question of whether increasing affluence (A) necessarily generates environmental degradation, and whether technological change (T) can decouple that relationship.

This is the terrain of the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC), another concept central to GY222. The EKC hypothesis, associated with Grossman and Krueger’s 1995 work, suggests an inverted-U relationship between income per capita and pollution. Degradation increases in early stages of development and eventually declines as countries grow wealthier. The lecture engages with this optimism directly. For some pollutants, the EKC story holds up. For carbon emissions and municipal solid waste, it notably does not. And for tropical deforestation, the trend line is not an inverted U but a one-way street moving relentlessly upward.

The Capital Framework

The conceptual heart of the lecture, and of Neumayer’s book, is a framework students already encounter in GY222, about the distinction between different forms of capital and their role in sustaining welfare across generations.

Drawing on Robert Solow’s economic definition of sustainability (leaving future generations “the capacity to be as well off as we are today”), the lecture sets up the central question in terms of a production function f(K, R), where K is physical capital and R is natural capital. The key analytical question is: what happens when R approaches zero? Can more K compensate? Students familiar with the GY222 treatment of factors of production (physical capital, labour and human capital, natural resources, and technology), can immediately recognise that this is the substitutability debate rendered formally.

Weak sustainability assumes K and R are substitutes. The total capital stock must be non-declining over time, but its composition can shift freely. On this view, depleting an oil field is acceptable so long as equivalent value is reinvested in, say, education or infrastructure. The mathematical implication is that consumption C must not decrease over time: C_t = C_{t+1}.

Strong sustainability treats K and R as complements rather than substitutes. In a Leontief-type production function (Y = K × R), if R = 0, then Y = 0 regardless of how much K is accumulated. Natural capital stock S must itself be maintained: S_t = S_{t+1}. The existing stock cannot be duplicated by manufactured capital because natural systems perform functions that no factory can replicate.

Two Paradigms

Where does the evidence land? On non-renewable resources, weak sustainability largely wins. Contrary to the “Limits to Growth” predictions of the early 1970s, which assumed no substitution and no technological change, there is no near-term risk of running out of oil, gas, or metals. The problem with fossil fuels is about climate, that there is far too much carbon in the grounde. Students studying the Limits to Growth debate in GY222 will find Neumayer’s response useful here: the dire predictions of the MIT model depended critically on its assumptions about substitutability and technological change, precisely the parameters the weak/strong sustainability debate contests.

On renewable resources and pollution, however, strong sustainability is more persuasive. Tropical primary forest loss is accelerating, with 2024 among the worst years on record. Scientists estimate that deforestation of 20–25% of the Amazon may be sufficient to trigger an irreversible tipping point, a shift to savanna-type vegetation, yet current deforestation sits at 14–17% and is rising. For carbon emissions, global temperatures are already on track to exceed 1.5°C of warming, with Neumayer predicting 3–3.5°C as a realistic outcome once positive feedback loops (including permafrost methane release) are accounted for.

Norway vs. the UK

A key practical implication of weak sustainability is that resource extraction rents must be invested. This distinction matters enormously. Consuming the proceeds of natural resource depletion is not sustainable even under weak sustainability assumptions; what matters is whether extraction revenues are channelled into other forms of capital that can sustain future welfare.

The Norway/UK comparison is instructive. Both countries extracted North Sea oil. Norway channelled revenues into a sovereign wealth fund, now exceeding $1 trillion in value. The UK did not adopt a comparable mechanism. From a weak sustainability standpoint, Norway’s approach is at least directionally correct; the UK’s consumption of its oil windfall is much harder to defend. This example is a useful illustration for exam purposes of what “investing rents” looks like in practice, and what failure to do so looks like.

The Discount Rate Problem and the Limits of CBA

One of the most analytically challenging sections of the lecture concerned the role of the discount rate in climate policy. The core issue is a temporal asymmetry: the costs of emission reduction fall on the present, while the benefits accrue far in the future. A high discount rate (consistent with current market rates of 4–5%) makes aggressive climate action appear unjustified in a standard cost-benefit framework. A low discount rate, as favoured by Nicholas Stern, makes it appear urgently necessary.

Neumayer’s contribution here is to argue that this framing may be the wrong one altogether. When the damages at stake include irreversible losses of non-substitutable natural capital the cost-benefit framework breaks down. It is of recognising that some things cannot be adequately captured in monetary present-value terms at all.

ESG, SDGs, and the Weak Sustainability Default

The lecture also touched on a question directly relevant to how sustainability is measured and governed in practice. ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) frameworks, Neumayer suggested, are essentially weak sustainability instruments. By aggregating heterogeneous indicators into composite scores, they obscure the distinction between capital types that can be traded off and those that cannot. The charge of greenwashing may be too blunt, but ESG as currently designed does not distinguish between substitutable and non-substitutable natural capital.

This connects to a broader theme in GY222: the three-pillar model of sustainable development (economic, social, environmental) and the Brundtland definition are both largely normative frameworks that leave unanswered the analytical question of substitutability. The SDGs similarly represent a weak sustainability orientation, treating all 17 goals as fungible priorities rather than identifying any as lexicographically prior.

Conclusion

Several angles:

The weak/strong sustainability debate maps onto real policy disagreements (Paris Agreement vs. binding emissions targets; EKC optimism vs. tipping point concerns). Neumayer’s point that neither paradigm is strictly falsifiable is analytically important: the debate is about making a persuasive case under uncertainty.

The production function formulation (f(K, R), substitutes vs. complements) provides a clean way to formalise the intuition behind weak and strong sustainability in economic terms, useful for any question on capital theory or intergenerational equity.

The discount rate debate (Stern vs. Nordhaus) is well-trodden ground, but Neumayer adds a deeper layer that even getting the discount rate right may not be sufficient if the losses involved are irreversible and non-substitutable. Cost-benefit analysis also has limits as a methodology.

The Norway case provides a concrete, empirically grounded example of what weak sustainability requires in practice and illustrates the political economy reasons why it so often fails.

Finally, the question of who bears the costs of transition, and who caused the problem in the first place, connects the weak/strong sustainability debate to questions of climate justice and North-South inequality that run through GY222.

entry.title: What Does It Mean to Be ‘Middle Class’?
entry.content:
The reflections here emerged from a recent lunchtime discussion with Prof. Mercer on middle-class formation in African cities, where I had the opportunity to raise questions about how we understand class across different cultural contexts.

The term “middle class” is ubiquitous in development discourse. It appears in policy briefs and newspaper headlines celebrating the rise of new consumer markets in Asia and Africa. However this seemingly straightforward category conceals an epistemological problem. What happens when the people we label as “middle class” do not recognise themselves in that term? And what does it mean for our analytical frameworks when this category is actively unspoken?

During a discussion on Tanzania, I learned that people do not use the term “middle class” in everyday conversation. There is no commonly deployed Swahili equivalent, one can translate it, of course, but the phrase does not circulate in the way it might in Ghana, India, or the United Kingdom. This absence is deeply rooted in Tanzania’s socialist history, specifically the ujamaa period under Julius Nyerere, during which the middle classes were ideologically positioned as enemies of the nation, parasites living off the labour of rural farmers, who were celebrated as the authentic owners of the Tanzanian state. Even today, unlike some African nations that proudly tout the size of their emerging middle class as evidence of developmental success, the Tanzanian state remains largely silent on the matter. The middle class exists but it exists without a name.

This raises a methodological challenge that I find compelling. If the people we study do not call themselves middle class, on what grounds do we, as researchers, impose that label? The response I encountered was twofold. First, one does not need to consciously name oneself as a class to be a class. Class can be performed through material practices, through the act of building a particular kind of house on the urban periphery, for instance, which signals a specific social position regardless of whether its owner articulates it in those terms. Second, the absence of class discourse is itself historically and politically significant. The silence is a product of specific ideological formations that made certain ways of speaking about society possible while foreclosing others. In this sense, the question is rather “what are the historical conditions under which class becomes speakable or unspeakable?”

This insight connects to broader debates in feminist and postcolonial scholarship about the politics of knowledge production. Just as feminist scholars like Donna Haraway have argued that all knowledge is situated and partial, so too must we recognise that analytical categories like “middle class” carry their own genealogies and assumptions. When we apply such categories to contexts where they do not emerge organically from local discourse, we risk imposing frameworks that obscure as much as they reveal. Yet abandoning the category entirely would mean losing a powerful tool for understanding how social stratification operates and reproduces itself. The challenge, then, is to hold both truths simultaneously, to remain attentive to the ways “class” travels and sometimes fails to translate.

What I found worth exploring is about the observation that most studies of middle-class formation capture a particular historical moment but rarely return to examine how things have changed. Leela Fernandes’s India’s New Middle Class (2006), for example, was published at a specific conjuncture, when India was embracing economic liberalisation and opening its markets to global capital. The book documented the emergence of a new consuming middle class at that precise moment. However nearly two decades later, no systematic restudy has traced how India’s middle class has evolved, how its interests have intersected with the rise of Hindutva nationalism, or how its composition has shifted with India’s changing role in the global economy. This is a potential direction for research about the temporal dimension of class formation.

There was also a fascinating observation about the instability of class markers. The material practices that once signalled middle-class status are constantly “trickling down” as consumer goods become more widely accessible. Take weddings as an example. Over the past three decades, wedding practices in Tanzania have transformed, tiered cakes, decorated halls, sparkly lights, and globalised music have become aspirational markers that can be partially replicated regardless of income level. One does not need the complete package; one can have something that gestures toward it, drawing ideas from Instagram and TikTok. The same applies to building materials, architectural flourishes, and household goods. Yet, crucially, having a fancy wedding cake does not make one middle class. The markers of distinction keep shifting, because they keep being appropriated. This creates an endless race for differentiation, a phenomenon that Pierre Bourdieu would recognise as the constant repositioning of social actors within a field of cultural capital.

Income-based approaches, while valuable for tracking changes over time, struggle to capture the relational and performative dimensions of class. In contexts where people have multiple income streams, such as a small grocery business or agricultural investments in rural areas, asking for a “monthly income” produces data that may be technically accurate but socially meaningless. Housing, by contrast, offers a material trace of class position that is literally visible and socially legible. The house speaks even when its owner does not. It also signals accumulation and social location in ways that income figures cannot.

This methodological point connects to a broader argument about how we might approach the study of class in the Global South. Rather than beginning with a predetermined category and searching for its local instantiation, we might instead begin with material practices. Moreover, the most productive research often comes not from confirming what we already suspect but from being genuinely surprised by what we find.

For those interested in pursuing research in this area, several directions seem promising. One approach would be to conduct a “restudy”, to return to a site where middle-class formation was documented fifteen or twenty years ago and ask what has changed. How do the dynamics of class-making at one historical conjuncture differ from those at another? What continuities persist beneath apparent transformations? Another direction would examine the politics of class discourse itself: why do some contexts produce active public discussion about the middle class while others suppress it? What are the political conditions under which class becomes visible or invisible as a category of public speech? A third possibility would trace the “trickle-down” of class markers over time, examining how specific material practices move through social strata and what new forms of distinction emerge to replace those that have been democratised.

This lunchtime reminded me that the categories we use to understand the social world are themselves products of that world. In Tanzania, the middle class builds houses, accumulates property, and reproduces itself through specific spatial practices, all without ever naming itself as such. Understanding why this is the case, and what it means for how we study class more broadly, would be questions worth pursuing.

entry.title: Rooms Without Outside
entry.content:
“Everything is possible, yet nothing is possible. Everything is permitted, yet nothing is permitted… Everything has an explanation, yet nothing has an explanation. Nothing is more valuable than anything else, and no idea is better than any other.” — E.M. Cioran, On the Heights of Despair

Prologue

September 2020, Changwon, South Korea. Police forced open the door of a small rented room. The handle had been tied shut from inside with rope. On the floor lay the decomposing bodies of a mother, 51, and her daughter, 22.

The walls were covered in hand-drawn pictures. The mother’s were colourful: symmetrical figures, two people facing each other, fashionably dressed, smiling. The daughter’s were black and white: anatomical diagrams, flowcharts of life and death, organs methodically labelled.

No one knows what happened inside. The coroner could not determine the cause of death and neighbours said they hadn’t seen either woman in months.

Psychiatry has a term for this: Shared Delusional Disorder, or Folie à deux. When one person’s delusional belief is adopted by someone in close relationship, the two construct a closed interpretive system together. Inside this system, everything is coherent: the outside world is dangerous, only each other can be trusted, and any attempt at intervention proves the threat is real.

A similar case occurred in the UK a few years ago. A Japanese family, three children, all graduates of elite universities lived together in complete isolation. When the eldest daughter died, the family wiped her body with alcohol, believing she was still alive. When police finally entered, the mother insisted that “She’s just sleeping.”

But this post is not about psychiatric pathology. I am interested in a more fundamental question: What happens when an interpretive system becomes completely closed, when it no longer allows any external input to alter itself? And more sharply: How do we determine who is deluded? On what grounds can science claim it is not simply another closed system?

When Judgement Loses Its Outside

Cioran’s passage is often read as nihilism. But looking again, he is not describing the absence but its excess of meaning.

“Everything has an explanation, yet nothing has an explanation.” This is a world with too much meaning. When all paths are permitted, no path leads anywhere. When everything can be explained, explanation loses its power to distinguish.

This is the condition of contemporary information environments. Online, any event generates countless explanations, from conspiracy theories to official narratives. Each has its own evidence chain and forms a system. The problem is thus that we have too much information and no shared criteria for judgement.

In such a world, “trust the science” is not an epistemological position. It is political, one that presumes an answer to the question it should be asking, that, who has the authority to define what counts as science?

Return to that room in Changwon. Psychiatry would diagnose the mother and daughter with Shared Delusional Disorder. This suggests their beliefs were “wrong.” However what makes a belief “delusional” rather than “conviction” or “theory”?

The traditional answer is that delusion is belief that contradicts reality. But this definition is circular. Who defines reality? By what standard?

I propose a different definition, that, delusion is belief that has lost its refutability.

In Changwon, the mother believed the outside world was dangerous. This belief is not inherently absurd as danger exists. The problem is that no evidence could disprove it. When neighbours knocked, it confirmed the threat. When the daughter wanted to go out, it showed she had been “contaminated.” Every potential counter-evidence was absorbed in advance as confirmation.

This is how closed systems operate, by having explanations so complete that nothing can enter from outside.

Thomas Kuhn argued that science does not progress linearly. It moves through cycles, from normal science, to crisis, to revolution, to new normal science.

During “normal science,” scientists work within a shared paradigm. They accept certain assumptions, use them to define valid questions and methods. In this sense, normal science resembles delusion as both depend on shared premises and maintain internal consistency.

But Kuhn identified a crucial difference, as in science, anomalies are allowed to accumulate. When enough phenomena resist explanation, the scientific community enters “crisis”, often with confusion and uncertainty. This crisis can eventually produce “paradigm shift” where a new set of assumptions replaces the old. And this is what delusion lacks. In that Changwon room, every discordant signal was immediately digested into the existing framework. No crisis was possible, therefore no revolution was possible. The system remained stable, until physical death ended everything.

Bruno Latour offered another perspective. Scientific facts are “solid” because they are supported by vast networks such as laboratories, peer review, funding bodies, and public trust. When any node in this network breaks, “facts” become unstable.

Latour is often misread as saying “science is fiction.” What he actually meant was that scientific objectivity is not given but achieved. Science is fragile. Its openness and capacity for self-correction all depend on specific social institutions and cultural conditions.

What happens when those conditions erode?

During COVID-19, “Follow the science” became a political slogan. The intention was good as in an environment flooded with misinformation, emphasise that expert judgement deserves respect. But the slogan contains a paradox.

Science deserves trust is because it does not demand unconditional trust. Its power comes from fallibility, meaning that any theory can be overturned by new evidence. As “trust the science” becomes a moral command, it betrays the spirit of science itself. More dangerously, when “science” is used to terminate discussion, it begins to exhibit the same structural features as delusion: irrefutable and intolerant of anomaly.

Argentine sociologist Adrián Scribano proposed, in his “sociology of hope,” a concept that seems unrelated but is in fact crucial.

Scribano argued that hope is not a psychological state or emotion, but a social structure. Specifically, hope is the experience that “the world has not yet been fully determined”, the capacity to remain open to the future.

Translated into epistemological terms: Hope = the possibility that interpretation can still be negotiated and rearranged.

Hope is the condition under which judgement systems remain open. When hope exists, we acknowledge our understanding is provisional to the future. When hope disappears, the world is “closed off” in advance as all answers already written. In this sense, delusion can be redefined as: belief that has lost the structure of hope. Becoming belief that no longer permits change.

The Changwon mother and daughter lost hope in the epistemological sense, of the possibility that the world might be different from what they believed. They chose a world that no longer changes, and death was merely the physical consequence.

The Second Room: Institutional Closure

Now let us enter another room.

England, 2024. Approximately 159,000 children live in “temporary accommodation”, hotels, hostels, converted shipping containers. The word “temporary” is misleading as average stays stretch into years, and some children spend their entire childhood in these spaces.

These rooms have no ropes tying door handles shut. But they are closed in a different way.

The housing crisis in England is not simply a shortage of homes. It is a system that produces and reproduces homelessness through interconnected policy mechanisms: Right to Buy depleted social housing stock (2 million units lost since 1980); replacement building never caught up; private rents rose; Local Housing Allowance was frozen; local councils, legally obligated to house children but chronically underfunded, turned to expensive temporary accommodation.

This is what journalist Dan Hewitt calls the “doom loop.” And the system is functioning exactly as designed.

Here is where the parallel with delusion becomes precise. Research by the Debt Trap Nation project reveals that 88% of English local authorities have housing debt disqualification rules. If a family owes rent arrears, often incurred because of housing instability, they can be barred from social housing waiting lists or have their priority reduced. In December 2023 alone, nearly 4,000 households were banned from bidding on social housing due to debt. 43% contained children. 5% had infants under two years old.

The debt is real but so was the structural violence that produced it. A mother fleeing domestic abuse may leave with nothing but debt. The years in temporary accommodation have no kitchen, so takeaway costs rise; children’s schools change repeatedly, so transport costs accumulate. The debt then becomes grounds for exclusion from stable housing, which generates more instability, which generates more debt.

This is a closed loop. But unlike the Changwon room, it is sealed by policy language. Every decision follows protocol and yet the cumulative effect is indistinguishable from a locked door.

Return to our earlier definition: delusion is belief that has lost its refutability. In the Changwon case, the mother’s belief, “the outside world is dangerous”, could not be disproven because every piece of counter-evidence was pre-absorbed into the system. In the housing system, the state’s implicit belief, “debt reflects individual responsibility”, operates identically. When a family’s poverty is caused by policy (frozen benefits, inadequate social housing, the five-week Universal Credit wait), this is recoded that “They should have budgeted better.”

The debt rules do not ask why a family is in debt. They only ask whether the debt exists, and then structure is dissolved into individual pathology. This is thus institutional delusion. No amount of evidence about structural causation can enter the assessment framework and change the outcome.

The Disappearance of Hope

Return now to Cioran: “All gains are losses, and all losses are gains.” This is nihilism as saturation, and Cioran’s despair is also, paradoxically, a kind of honesty. He refuses the false comfort of premature closure, the delusion that we have found the answer, the system, the truth that ends all questioning.

The danger is what happens when institutions adopt the opposite stance while producing the same effect by claiming certainty while systematically eliminating the possibility of revision.

Hope, as I have defined it, is not optimism. It is the structural condition under which change remains possible(the willingness to be proven wrong). When hope dies in a family, we get Changwon. When hope dies in an institution, we get something harder to see but no less lethal: 159,000 children in “temporary” accommodation that has no exit.

Lauren Berlant called this cruel optimism: attachment to conditions that actually prevent flourishing. The families in temporary accommodation are told to be patient and to trust the process. However this is not hope but just a hope’s simulation, maintaining the appearance of openness while foreclosing.

Reopening the Room

If delusion is the collapse of refutability, then the task is not to find the “correct” belief but to rebuild the conditions under which beliefs can be changed. For science, it means authority must remain contestable. For epistemology more broadly, it means that hope must be institutionalised, as the structural commitment to keeping the world undetermined, to maintaining spaces where anomaly can accumulate and where judgement can be revised.

Conclusion

I began with a question: How do we determine who is deluded?

The answer is: we cannot determine this from any position of perfect externality. We are always inside some interpretive system. But this does not mean all systems are equivalent. The difference here is what the system does with doubt.

A delusion seals itself against doubt. On the other hand, living system metabolises doubt, allows it to produce crisis and change. The mother in Changwon tied the door handle with rope and the housing system ties the door with policy language. Both claim to be protecting something but both produce rooms without outside.

The task is therefore to ensure that doors, all doors, can still be opened, and with an outside.
